Civil Revision No. 551 of 1997
with
Civil Revision No. 705 of 1997
lawyer:
No one ------ for the petitioner in both the Rules. 
Mr. M. A. Jalil, Advocate  ------- for opposite parties in both Rules.
parties:
Mustafizur Rahman
Vs.
Most. Farida Yasmin and others
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Aziz, J: Both the Rules issued in Civil Revision Nos.551/1997 and 705/1997 are directed against the same impugned judgment and decree dated 4.11.1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No.145/1993 setting aside and reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.7.1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rampal, Bagerhat in Title Suit No.60 of 1988 dismissing the suit.

2. Short fact leading to these Rules is that the opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.60/1988 on 28.4.1988 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rampal, Bagerhat for partition on declaration of their title in the suit land stating, inter alia, that the suit land recorded in C.S. Khatian No.89 originally belonged to Kenai Sheikh who died leaving a grandson Ansar Ali Sheikh and a daughter Fatema Khatun who succeeded 2'59 acres and 1'30 acres respectively of the lands left by him. Fatema Khatun gifted her said 110 acres of land by a Heba dated 19.01.1960 to her father Ayezuddin. Ayezuddin and Ansar Ali transferred the entire 3'89 acres of land by a Patta dated 4.7.1953 to one Syed Ali Fakir for a limited period and Ansar Ali later got his land re-transferred in the name of his son Ali Akbar and took back the Patta. Ansar Ali and Ayezuddin by executing Kabala dated 5.12.1957 sold 1'98 decimals of land to plaintiff nos.1 and 2, namely, Farida Yasmin and Raisa Yasmin and Ayezuddin sold 1'86 decimals of land to plaintiff no.1 by executing another Kabala but they could not register the deed on that day and taking advantage of same filed Title Suit Nos. 543/1958 and 544/1958 for Specific Performance of Contract through their relations Shamsuddin Patwary which was contested by one Rustam Ali, the plaintiff no.1 and the suit ended in dismissal. The plaintiff got the deed register through the District Registrar on 10.3.1959 under Serial Nos.1870 and 1871 against Ansar and Ayezuddin and possessed the land. Ansar Sheikh by Kabala dated 26.9.59 sold '25 decimals of land to Etim Sheikh who in his turn sold the same to plaintiff no.1 vide registered Kabala dated 11.6.1964. The plaintiff thus acquired 3'53 acres of land. The defendant no.1 (Ansar Sheikh) possessed '36 decimals of land and the plaintiff has homestead covering an area of '96 decimals of land in Plot No.327 excluding '13 decimals of that Plot and the eldest daughter of the plaintiff with her husband resides in that homestead. The further case of the plaintiffs is that they are possessing the suit land by purchase and paying rents mutating their names. But in the S.A. record the name of Ansar Sheikh was recorded wrongly along with their names and although the said wrong recording did not cause any inconvenience in their enjoyment and possession of the suit land but when they demanded partition of the suit land to the defendants on coming to know of the wrong recording on 7.4.1988 and claimed partition they refused to do so. Hence they brought the suit.

3. Defendant No.1 Ansar Ali Sheikh, the Petitioner in Civil Revision No.705/1997 and the defendant no.3 Mustafizur Rahman, the petitioner of Civil Revision No.551/1997 contested the suit by filing separate written statements denying the material averments of the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable, the suit is barred by limitation and defect for parties, etc. admitting that the suit land originally belonged to Kenai Sheikh who died leaving the defendant-petitioner as his grandson and a daughter Fatema Khatun who inherited his land as stated in the plaint. The further case of the defendant no.1, the petitioner in Civil Revision No.705/1997 is that the suit land was put to mortgage for a period of 15 years and after expiry of the term of mortgage the suit land was returned to its original owners Ayezuddin and Ansar Ali Sheikh and they never sold the suit property to the plaintiffs or Etim Ali Sheikh and even if any sale-deed is produced by the plaintiff the same should be treated as forged and false and not binding upon them.

4. The further case of the defendant no.3 petitioner in Civil Revision No.551/97 is that after the death of Kenai Sheikh 3'89 acres of suit land devolved upon defendant no.1 Ansar Ali Sheikh and his sister Fatema Khatun who were in possession of the suit land in Plot No.327 as per their respective share. Defendant No.1 owned and possessed 3'58 acres of land exclusively by amicable partition and the suit land was never sold to either plaintiff nos.1 and 2 or to Etim Sheikh nor they were inducted into possession of the same. The defendant no.3 also made same written statements that any such deed if produced in Court that should be created as forged and false and not binding upon the defendant, etc.

5. Trial Court framed as many as 7 issues for decision in the suit and a total number of 10 witnesses were examined by the parties and produced documents which were marked exhibits. On consideration of the evidence on record the trial Court dismissed the suit for defect of parties and for not bringing all the properties of the suit Khatian in the hotchpotch of the suit.

6. On appeal by the plaintiffs-opposite parties the appellate Court below decreed the suit setting aside and reversing the judgment' and decree of the trial Court in Title Appeal No.145/1993. Hence these Rules.

7. None appears in support of either of the Rules.

8. It may be stated that originally the suit was filed by Rustam Ali and his deceased wife Jobeda Khatun, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs with the prayer for declaration of title in the suit schedules Ka, Ga and Gha properties and for permanent injunction with a prayer for recovery of Khas possession of Gha schedule property which was dismissed on contest in trial. On the appeal preferred by them the earlier judgment and decree of the trial Court was set aside and the case was sent back on remand to the trial Court for retrial with some directions. During retrial the plaintiffs amended their plaint by inserting the present prayer on amending some earlier statements.

9. Perused the judgments of the Courts below. The trial Court found the suit maintainable in its present form and that the suit was not barred by limitation, but dismissed the suit for defect of parties and for not bringing the entire lands of the suit Khatian in the hotchpotch of the suit. On the other hand the appellate Court below decreed the suit setting aside and reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court finding that the entire lands in the suit Khatian need not be brought in the hotchpotch except the lands owned and possessed are in dispute between the parties. The appellate Court also reversed the finding of the trial Court on non-maintainability of the suit for defect of parties finding that the parties in dispute for partition having been impleaded in the suit and the finding of the trial Court being that the suit is maintainable in its present form, the trial Court wrongly dismissed the suit for defect of parties contradicting its own finding.

<u>10. The finding of the appellate Court below that all the joint properties need not be brought in the hotchpotch of the partition suit unless it is proved that the parties in dispute would be prejudiced by such omission, although-general principle is to include the entire properties of all the co-sharers, does not suffer from any infirmity nor erred in law in coming to said finding resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The appellate Court below came to the aforesaid finding relying on the decisions in the case between Mainuddin Biswas & ors. Vs. Sohrab Ali Mir & ors., reported in 5 DLR 544 and in the case between Md.Shahidul Alam Khan Vs. Md. Gulzar Alam, reported in 36 DLR 290. The finding of the lower appellate Court as aforesaid is also supported by a decision in the case between Safaruddin and others Vs. Fazlul Huq and others, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151.</u>

<u>11. In consideration of the same, I am of the opinion that the general rule of including all the lands of the co-sharers in the hotchpotch is not inflexible one and can be relaxed in appropriate cases if such omission does not cause any prejudice to any of the parties in dispute. There is no such allegation in the instant case making the suit liable for dismiss on that ground and as such the trial Court has committed wrong in dismissing the suit. There is also no specific evidence and materials on record that the suit is defect for non-impleading any necessary party and as such the appellate Court below has rightly found that the trial Court has wrongly dismissed the suit for defect of parties. The appellate Court came to it's own and independent finding in reversing the finding and setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court on due and proper consideration of the facts and materials on record of the case which does not justify any interference by this Court.</u>

12. In consideration of my above discussions and finding I find no merit in either of the Rules and those are liable to be discharged.

13. In the result, the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below is hereby upheld.

14. The order of stay passed earlier by this Court in both the Rules are hereby vacated.

15. Send down the lower Court records expeditiously.

End.

parties:
Nawab Khaja Habibullah Askari & others ------ Petitioners 
Vs
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This Rule has been obtained upon an application filed under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents Nos.1-5 to show cause as to why they should not be directed to release the Estate of late Nawab of Dhaka Khaja Salimullah Bahadur from the custody of Court of Wards in favour of the petitioners (4 in all) and respondent Nos. 6-8, 10-34, 36-39 and 41-47.

2. In support of the prayer of having the properties, as claimed to have been of late Nowab of Dhaka Khaja Salimullah, released from the custody of Court of Wards petitioners have stated, inter alia, that said Nowab mortgaged some properties to Raja Sreenath Roy and others of Bhaggapur and also to Raja Sreenath Roy; that the mortgage suit Nos. 12 of 1907 and 16 of 1907 were instituted by the mortgagees in the Court of First Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and they obtained decree therein; that the Nowab having found himself in a precarious financial predicament to satisfy the mortgage decrees applied for a loan of Taka 14 lakh to the Government of India, that the Secretary of State for India considered the application of the Nawab in council and communicated Government of India's decision to grant loan against the security of the movable and immovable properties of Nowab, that a mortgage deed was drawn and executed on 6th August, 1908 between the Court of Wards 1st Part and the Nowab in the second part and the Secretary of State for India in the third part; that by the aforesaid mortgage deed movable and immovable properties described in the schedule to the mortgage deed were mortgaged for satisfaction of debt of Taka 14 lakh out of which Taka 3,11,500 was paid by the Collector of Dhaka as purchase money together with incidental cost for repayment and purchase of mortgage decrees of Raja Sreenath Roy and others and adjusted, as such, against the said loan; that mortgage deed provided for repayment of debt with interest at the stipulated rate within 30 years by the Court of Wards. It was further stipulated in the mortgage deed, that neither the said ward nor his heirs, successors, executors, administrator and assigns shall be able to take back any of the property mortgaged from the custody of the Court of Wards as long as the whole amount of mortgaged money is not repaid; that 30 years period expired on 6-7-1938 and thereafter, another 57 years passed from August, 1938 but the property is still retained by the Court of Wards. It has been alleged that the Court of Wards did not furnish any statement of accounts of the repayment of debt either to the Nawab or to any of his heirs or successors and, as such, the petitioners and the respondent Nos. 6-8, 10-34, 36-39 and 41-47 are quite in the dark about the matter of repayment of loan. It has been contended by the petitioners that they have reasonable cause to believe that out of the income of the mortgage property the loan of Taka 14 lakh had already been paid and the Court of Wards has been arbitrarily and illegally continuing the possession of the property mortgaged by the mortgage deed dated 6th August, 1908.

3. Respondent Nos. 2 and 5—The Chairman, Land Reform Board and the Chief Manager of Court of Wards—respectively have entered appearances and have filed affidavit-in-opposition. These respondents upon denying the correctness of the material averments made in the writ petition have stated, inter alia, that the title i.e. Nowab, is not an inheritable one and that the claim of the petitioners as of being Nawab is unfounded and unsustainable one; that the claim of the petitioners that they and respondents Nos. 6-8, 10-34, 36-39 and 41-47, hereinafter referred to as said respondents, are the present sole exclusive heirs/successors is not correct, that neither the petitioners nor the said respondents had established their claim of inheritance and succession by any cogent evidence before the Court of Wards; that the petitioners nor the said respondents have filed any papers showing that they are the sole proprietor of the property which was placed under the management of the Court of Wards; that almost 50% of the wards of the original owner had left Bangladesh and that their whereabouts were not known, as such, their property has assumed the character of abandoned property and that vested in the Government as per provision of President's Order No.16 of 1972; that the said respondents have not filed any paper before the Court of Wards in support of their claim of being proprietor of the property managed by the Court of Wards, nor they have approached the Court of Wards seeking release of the property from the management thereof, that joint proprietorship has not been partitioned and, as such, the Court of Wards in the absence of determination of share of the petitioners as well as the said respondents and other proprietors of the property, in law, cannot release the property to the petitioners and the said respondents, that the petitioners have not made any statement as to how the mortgaged properties were redeemed and discharged from the mortgage debt, nor the petitioners have given any particulars and description of the property which was the subject matter of the mortgage; that it is not correct that the Court of Wards did not furnish any statement of account of repayment of debt either to the Nowab Khaja Salimullah Bahadur or to any of his heirs or successors, or it is correct that the petitioners and the said respondents were ignored about the matter; that the petitioners' contention of repayment of loan out of income of the mortgaged property and that even after repayment and disbursement of amount for which the property was mortgaged the Court of Wards was retaining the possession of the mortgaged property illegally is not correct; that it is not correct that before and after acquisition of rent receiving interest the officers of the Court of Wards in collusion with designing persons leased out, sold and otherwise disposed of various moveable and immovable mortgaged properties and mis-appropriated wholly or partly the proceeds of the mortgage property, that as there is ample provision under the Court of Wards Act for adjudication of the dispute of the kind as stated in the writ petition and that the petitioners having had not resorted to that forum the writ petition so filed is not maintainable; that it has not been established by any competent Court that the petitioners as well as the said respondents are the heirs and successors of Nowab of Dhaka Khaja Salimullah Bahadur and that they are the proprietors of the estate jointly or individually; that the matter of succession to the property of the estate by the petitioners and the said respondent being a disputed question and, as such, the Court of Wards cannot release the property until the dispute is resolved or determined by a competent Civil Court, that the petitioners ought to have reported to the Court of Wards for settlement of their claim in respect of the property in the light of the provision of the Court of Wards Act; that as there is conflicting claim amongst the wards and that joint proprietorship as has not been partitioned, the Court of Wards cannot release the property in favour of the petitioners and the said respondents.

4. Petitioners have filed Affidavit-in-Reply to the Affidavit-in-Opposition of the respondent Nos.2 and 5 denying the material averments made therein and reiterating the statements made in the writ petition. Learned Advocate for the petitioner No.1 has submitted that the amount, i.e. Taka 14 lath, for which the property was mortgaged for 30 years as has been repaid or satisfied between the period for which the property was mortgaged and that by the time that has lapsed after the expiry of the period for which the property was mortgaged, but still then as the property is being retained by the Court of Wards, said retention of the property by the Court of Wards is not only illegal but also arbitrary one. Learned Advocate appearing for the added petitioner Nos. 2-4 has adopted the submission of the leaned Advocate appearing for the petitioner No.1.

5. Although no affidavit-in-opposition was filed on behalf of respondent No.1, the Secretary, Ministry of Land, the learned Assistant Attorney-General with the leave of the Court made submission on point of law. Learned Assistant Attorney-General has submitted that the statements made in support of the prayer for releasing of the property that was mortgaged in 1908 as needs adjudication after scrutiny of contending facts and that, as such, the forum for such adjudication being the civil Court the petitioners ought to have sought for their redress in the civil Court at first and that further, as adjudication of the disputed facts is not permissible in a writ proceeding, the writ petition so filed and the Rule so obtained thereupon is liable to be discharged.

6. Learned Advocate for the respondent Nos.2 and 5 submitted that unless there is adjudication as regard the matter of satisfaction of the debt or repayment of the debt for the satisfaction whereof the property was mortgaged and that, if on such adjudication, it is found that the debt for which the property that was mortgaged in 1908 has been satisfied or repaid, only then there comes the question of releasing the property from the custody of the Court of Wards and there being no such adjudication relief that has been sought in the writ petition is not available or that cannot be granted or, in other words, the petitioners cannot have the relief as sought in the writ petition; that in the absence of determination of identity of the claimants of the property and that in the absence of adjudication of claim of the petitioners as well as the said respondents and the other persons who have filed applications for being added as party in the category of respondents, the property cannot be released to the petitioners and the said respondents alone and, as such, prayer for release of the property to the petitioners and the said respondents is liable to be rejected. Learned Advocate continues that almost 50% of the claimants of the property were absent or, in other words, left Bangladesh immediately at the time of liberation war of Bangladesh and immediately after emergence of Bangladesh and consequently, their shares having had assumed the character of abandoned property and thereupon having had vested in the government, petitioners and the said respondents' claim of being owner of the property and their prayer for releasing the property from the management of the Court of Wards is not legally tenable in the absence of determination how much of the property has assumed the character of abandoned property and that to how much quantity of the property petitioners and the said respondents are entitled or that they can lay their claim legally; that there being stipulation in the mortgage deed that unless the mortgaged debt is satisfied or paid the property would not be released from the management of the Court of Wards and that there being no determination that the debt which was to be satisfied or repaid had been satisfied or repaid by this time the prayer for release of the property merits no consideration.

7. Petitioners have filed the writ petition seeking release of the property which was placed under the management of the Court of Wards on the application of Nawab of Dhaka Khaja Salimullah Bahadur and that the said property was mortgaged jointly by the Nawab and the Court of Wards to the Secretary of State for India for repayment of the debt of Taka 14 lakh of the Nawab. It is the contention of the petitioners that the mortgage was made in 1908 for a period of 30 years as security towards the payment of Taka 14 lakh and that the said amount of Taka 14 lakh since 1908 and by the time till the date of filing of the writ petition has been repaid or satisfied and, as such, the petitioners and the said respondents being the heirs and successors in interest of the Nawab are entitled to have the property released from the management of Court of Wards. Against the aforesaid contention of the petitioners and the said respondents, the respondent Nos.2 and 5 have submitted that matter as to repayment or satisfaction of the debt needs adjudication on investigation of complicated facts and that that having not been done and that also no material having been placed in the writ petition in support of the claim of the petitioners that the mortgage debt has been satisfied, as such, relief that has been sought in the writ petition cannot be had to the petitioners or, in other words, writ petition cannot be maintained by the petitioners. Respondent Nos. 2 and 5 have also contended that part of the property that was placed under the management of the Court of Wards has become abandoned property and that in the absence of determination as to how much of the property has become abandoned property, petitioners' prayer for releasing the property to them that was placed under management of the Court of Wards by the mortgage deed of the year 1908 cannot be entertained.

8. In the writ petition except making statements of general nature that the amount for repayment of which the property was mortgaged has been repaid or satisfied by this time no material have been placed on record wherefrom it can be seen as to whether in fact the amount for which the property was mortgaged has been repaid to the third party in the mortgage deed i.e. Government. In our view, as determination of question of repayment of the debt, for which the property was mortgaged, to the third party i.e. Secretary of State for India, later on Government of Pakistan and that since 1971 Government of Bangladesh, is a matter of going into detailed accounting as well as scrutiny of complicated and contentious facts which is not permissible in the instant proceeding and that as in the absence of determination of the fact of repayment or satisfaction of the debt or the amount for which the property was mortgaged it cannot be said that in the meantime the amount for which the property was mortgaged has been paid back to the Secretary of State for India (3rd party) or that thereafter to the successor states or Governments, as such, relief sought for by the petitioner is not available to them. There is no material on record where-from it can be seen that the petitioners or any other claimants of the property ever approached the Court of Wards for determination of the fact of repayment of the debt for which the property as managed by the Court of Wards was mortgaged. Since in the absence of determination of the fact of repayment of debt for which the property was mortgaged there cannot be any question of releasing the property from the management of the Court of Wards and that the petitioner having not placed any reliable material on record where-from it can be seen that the amount for which the property was mortgaged has been repaid by this time to the 3rd party in the mortgaged deed, in such state of the matter we are of the opinion that in the absence of determination of the fact of repayment of the amount for which the property was mortgaged petitioners prayer for releasing the property from the management of the Court of Wards is not entertainable in law.

9. As regard the claim of the respondent Nos. 2 and 5 that some portion of the property that was placed in the management of the Court of Wards and that later on mortgaged in 1908 have become abandoned property, it appears that same is contrived on the part of the said respondents to deprive the claimants of the property and that to continue the management of the mortgaged property in case of repayment or satisfaction of debt, since no material has been placed on record in support of the claim of the respondent Nos. 2 and 5 that part of the property has become abandoned property. The said respondents have also not filed any paper showing that the said property has been listed as abandoned property and published in the official gazette under the provision of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985. In that background of the matter we are of the view that the claim of the respondent Nos. 2 and 5 that some portion of the property that was placed in the management of the Court of Wards and later on mortgaged in 1908 has become abandoned property is not legally sustainable.

10. Application that was filed in August, 1997 with the prayer for addition of party in the category of respondents but remained pending till the date of hearing of Writ petition has been considered by us. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate, appeared to press the application and made his submission in support of prayer for being added as respondents in the writ petition.

11. As seen from the application for addition of party that the applicants are claiming themselves as the successor to the property managed by the Court of Wards and are opposing the release of the property from the management of the Court of Wards. This shows that applicants are claiming themselves as the proprietors of the property that was placed under the management of the Court of Wards and that later on mortgaged in 1908 and, as such, the claim so made needs adjudication for the determination of the fact as to whether they are the sole claimants of the property i.e. the applicants who have filed application for being added as respondents and opposing the prayer for releasing of the property or that there are other claimant too to the property as managed by the Court of Wards.

12. In that view of the matter we are of the opinion that the applicants need not be added as party in the writ petition as the respondents.

<u>13. Since we have already held that in the absence of adjudication of the matter as to whether the debt, for the repayment whereof the property was mortgaged has been repaid or satisfied by this time and that as there are contentious claims of the parties as to proprietorship of the property that was placed in the management of the Court of Wards and that later on mortgaged in 1908 for securing payment of debt of Taka 14 lakh to the Secretary of State for India (3rd party in the mortgage deed), the property cannot be released from the management of the Court of Wards and, as such, we are of the opinion that petitioner's prayer for release of the property from the management of the Court of Wards is not legally entertain able.</u>

Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

Mrs. Zakia Doha
Vs.
Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement (in W. P. No. 2603 of 2000)
And
Mrs. Zakia Doha
Vs.
Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (In W.P. No. 1042 of 2001)

Mrs. Atia Siddiqui
Vs.
The Govt. of People & ors (In W.P. No. 5721 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury, J: In Writ Petition No. 2603 of 2000, a Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 25.11.1996 (Annexure-J) passed by the Court of Settlement, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka (respondent No. 1) rejecting the prayer of the petitioner for release of the property situated at NER-14, Road No. 84, Gulshan, Dhaka from the 'Ka' list of abandoned properties should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. In Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001, a Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents as to why the impugned auction notice dated 16.03.2001 (Annexure-K) published by the respondent No. 1 RAJUK so far it relates to the petitioner's property situated at NER-14. Road No. 84, Gulshan, Dhaka as an abandoned property should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

3. Both the Writ Petition nos. 2603 of 2000 and 1042 of 2001 have been heard together. In the midst of hearing, the learned Assistant Attorney-General Mr. Md. Abdul Kader Talukder (as he was then) made a prayer for hearing of the Writ Petition No. 5721 of 1997 together with the other Writ Petitions inasmuch as the case property is one and the same and the prayer was allowed. However, this consolidated judgment disposes of all the 3 (three) Writ Petitions.

4. In Writ Petition no. 2603 of 2000, the petitioner's case, is short, is as follows:

The Petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha is a Bangladeshi national who was married to late J.R.S. Doha in 1959 and since then she has been living in Bangladesh without any inter-mission. However, on 8thJune, 1965, the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) now re-named as Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (RAJUK) executed a 99 years' lease agreement in favour of the full sister of the petitioner, namely, Mrs. Atia Siddiqui for a plot of land measuring 1(one) bigha and 4(four) kattas sitauted a SE(K)-14, Road No. 84, Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka and in due course, Mrs. Atia Siddiqui got delivery of possession of the said plot of land. Thereafter she constructed a two-storied building thereon which was leased out to the Deputy Indian High Commission by an agreement dated 07.01.1970 at a monthly rental of Tk. 2500/-and it is still the official residence of the Indian High Commissioner. On 14.12.1970, the owner Mrs. Atia Siddiqui out of natural love and affection made an oral gift of the case property to the petitioner in presence of witnesses according to the Mohammedan Law and handed over the relevant papers in respect of the said property to the donee which she accepted. On the self-same date, the donor Mrs. Atia Siddiqui made a written declaration of the oral gift which was attested by those witnesses. Subsequently, the donor took the donee to the Deputy Indian High Commissioner and handed over the papers relating to the gift to him and requested him to attorney her as the land lady and pay rent to her by virtue of the declaration of the deed of gift dated 14.12.1970, The officers of the Indian High Commission requested the petitioner and her sister to wait for some time to complete the formalities under intimation to the Government of India. However, on 25.05.1972, the petitioner applied to the DIT for mutation of her name; but to her utter surprise, she came to know that the case property had been declared an abandoned property. She approached the Indian High Commission for providing her with monthly rent, but It did not do so. Mrs. Atia Siddiqui also wrote to the Indian High Commission to that effect from U.K, but the High Commission wrote back to her on 15.09.1975 informing that rent was being paid to the Government and advised her to be in touch with the Government. Anyway, there were series of correspondences between the petitioner and the relevant authorities about the release of the case property, but in vain. Eventually, the petitioner filed Case No. 336 of 1988 in the Court of Settlement, Dhaka praying for release of the case property from the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings which was published in the official Gazette on 23.09.1986. The Court of settlement by its judgment and order dated 25.11.1996 rejected the claim of the petitioner on the grounds, inter alia, that the gift was not acted upon and that 30 days' prior notice of transfer and prior payment of transfer fee were not made in favour of the DIT as stipulated in Clause 23 of the deed of lease dated 08.06.1965 and that the property is an abandoned property. During the War of Liberation in 1971, the Indian High commission was closed for some time and after the emergence of Bangladesh, it got back the possession of the case property. The oral gift made by Mrs. Atia Siddiqui in favour of the petitioner is a valid gift in accordance with the Mohammedan Law. The petitioner has been the legal owner of the property since 14.10.1970. As the owner of the case property, the petitioner has been in this country all along since 1970 and that being so the same cannot be enlisted as an abandoned property by any stretch of imagination. The Indian High Commission has been the tenant in the case property firstly under the donor Mrs. Atia Siddiqui and thereafter under the donee, the present petitioner. On the date of promulgation of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972, the whereabouts of the petitioner were known to the Government and as such, the treatment of the case property as an abandoned property is de hors the law. Hence the Rule.

5. The case of the respondent no. 2 in Writ petition No. 2603 of 2000 as disclosed in its affidavit-in-opposition, in short, is as follows:

It is true that the original owner of the case property and elder sister of the petitioner, that is to say, Mrs. Atia Siddiqui got the case property by way of lease from the then DIT on 08.06.1965. But it is not a fact that Mrs. Atia Siddiqui made an oral gift of the case property in favour of the petitioner on 14.10.1970 under the Mohammedan Law. Mrs. Atia Siddiqui did not make any written declaration of the alleged oral gift either. However, during the War of Liberation, 1971, she went to Pakistan and lived there. She did never come back to Bangladesh. So the case property was legally and validly declared an abandoned property under the P.O. No. 16 of 1972. The petitioner forged the written declaration of the alleged oral gift. Since the alleged oral gift is invalid in law, the petitioner cannot be the legal owner of the case property. Under Mrs. Atia Siddiqui, the Indian High Commission was in possession of the property in question as her tenant. But during the War of Liberation in 1971, it was left uncared-for by the Indian High Commission and after the War of Liberation, the High Commission took over its possession once again. The petitioner has no right, title, interest and possession in the case property. As such, the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

6. The case of the respondent no. 3 in Writ Petition No. 2603 of 2000 as set out its affidavit-in-opposition, in brief, is as follows:

The case property was leased out to Mrs. Atia Siddiqui on 8d' June, 1965 by the then DIT under certain stipulations. But during the War of Liberation in 1971, she started residing in Pakistan and never returned to Bangladesh. So the case property is an abandoned property by operation of law. The alleged oral gift was never acted upon by taking over possession of the case property by the petitioner. She has been trying to grab the property by creating and ante-dating some forged documents. Besides, the alleged gift of the case property in favour of the petitioner by her elder sister Mrs. Atia Siddiqui is illegal in view of the provisions of Clause 23 of the deed of lease. The Government has been possessing the case property through the Indian High Commission as an allottee thereunder. However, the petitioner attempted to get her name mutated in the records of the DIT (now RAJUk) submitting some fishy documents; but ultimately, her prayer for mutation was turned down. The 'Government legally and validly took over possession of the case property under the relevant provisions of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 before enlisting the same as an abandoned property. The Indian High Commission has been paying rent to the Government as its allottee. The petitioner is not entitled to get any relief in the Writ Petition. As such, the rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

7. In Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001, the case of the petitioner, in brief, is as under:

The case property was leased out to Mrs: Atia Siddiqui on 8th June, 1965 for a period of 99 years by the then DIT. Anyway, on 07.01.1970, the said property was leased out in favour of the Indian High Commission by an agreement for a period of 5 years. On 14.12.1970, Mrs. Atia Siddiqui orally gifted the case property in favour, of the petitioner. In spite of several attempts, the petitioner failed to get her name mutated in the records of the DIT. Ultimately under compelling circumstances, she filed Case No. 336 of 1988 in the 1st Court of settlement, Dhaka for release of the case property which was published in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings in the official Gazette on 23.09.1986. But the Court of Settlement rejected the claim of the petitioner. All of a sudden, the respondent no. 1 RAJUK published an auction notice on 16.03.2001 in "The Daily Janakantha' inviting applications for sale of the case property along with other properties and the last date for submission of bids was 28.03.2001. By virtue of the oral gift under the Mohammedan Law, the petitioner has been the actual owner of the case property and as such, the same cannot be auction-sold by the respondent no. 1. Hence the Rule.

8. The case of the respondent no. 1 in Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001 as disclosed in its affidavit-in-opposition, in brief, is as follows:

The case property is an abandoned property within the meaning of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972. The alleged oral gift of the said property by Mrs. Atia Siddiqui in favour of the petitioner is not legally valid. So the petitioner is not the lawful owner of the case property by way of gift from the original owner Mrs. Atia Siddiqui. The 1st Court of Settlement, Dhaka lawfully dismissed the case of the petitioner and affirmed the enlistment of the case property in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings. As an abandoned property, the RAJUK, under the authority of the Government, decided to auction sell the same and invited applications for that purpose and the bid of the added respondent no. 3 was accepted by the RAJUK as the highest bidder. The case property being an-abandoned property is liable to be auction-sold in pursuance of the auction notice floated by the RAJUK. So the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

9. The case of the added-respondent no. 3 in Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001 as set out in his affidavit-in-opposition, in short, runs as follows:

The case property was rightly declared an abandoned property on the ground that the owner Mrs. Atia Siddiqui was not available in Bangladesh as a Bangladeshi citizen at the time of commencement of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972. Subsequently, the Court of Settlement, Dhaka by its judgment and order dated 25.11.1996 upheld the treatment of the property in question as an abandoned property. However, on 29.11.1999, the Government constituted a committee for sale of abandoned properties. Thereafter by a Memo dated 15.03.2000, the Ministry of Works asked the RAJUK to take necessary steps for auction sale of abandoned properties including the case property. Accordingly, the respondent no. 1-RAJUK published an auction notice on 16.03.2001 inviting bids for sale of the properties. In response to the auction notice floated by the RAJUK, the respondent no. 3 submitted a bid for purchase of the case property for a sum of Tk. 6,36,84,600/- along with earnest money of Tk. 25,00,000/- by a bank draft dated 28.03.2001 of the Standard Chartered Bank payable to the Chairman, RAJUK, Dhaka upon fulfilling all relevant terms and conditions. The bid of the added-respondent no. 3 was found to be the highest and accordingly, it was accepted by the RAJUK Technical Committee. Afterwards the RAJUK by its letter dated 22.04.2001 informed the added-respondent no. 3 that his offer being the highest was accepted with a request to deposit the balance amount of Tk. 6,11,84,600/- by 21.05.2001 in the account of the RAJUK with Janata Bank, RAJUK Bhaban, Dhaka. As he as in the process of depositing the balance amount in the account of the RAJUK pursuant to the letter dated 22.04.2001, he came to learn about the writ petition and the stay order passed therein. Be that as it may, he wrote a letter dated 30.04.2001 to the RAJUK intimating that in view of the stay-order of the High Court Division, it was not advisable for him to deposit the balance amount. Anyway, the RAJUK by its letter dated 14.05.2001 informed him that in view of the Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001 file by Mrs. Zakia Doha and the interim-order passed therein, further steps following the RAJUK's letter dated 22.04.2001 had been stayed. The added-respondent no. 3, being the highest bidder and his bid having been accepted, is entitled to auction-purchase the case property from the RAJUK as per auction notice dated 16.03.2001. So the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

10 We have perused the Writ Petitions, Affidavits-in-Opposition and the relevant Annexures annexed thereto and heard the learned Advocates for the parties in extenso.

11. The High Court Division exercising power under Article 102 of the Constitution does not work as a Court of Appeal and as such it is not required to make determination of facts on its own. It can interfere with the findings of a Court of facts under its extra-ordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it can be shown that the Court has acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence/facts causing prejudice to the petitioner or it has acted malafide or in violation of the principle of natural justice. This view is underpinned by the decision in the case of the Government of Bangladesh Appellant-...Vs... Md. Jalil and others..  Respondents reported 15BLD (AD)175=49DLR(AD)26.

12. However, at the outset, Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha, submits that the oral gift in respect of the case property made by the original owner Mrs. Atia Siddiqui in favour of her younger sister Mrs. Zakia Doha on 14.12.1970 under the Mohammedan Law is a valid gift and since at the relevant time, the Indian High Commission was in its occupation as a tenant under Mrs. Atia Siddiqui, the petitioner got its constructive delivery of possession under the oral gift.

13. Mr. T.H. Khan further submits that as the petitioner is the legal owner for the case property on the strength of the oral gift dated 14.12.1970 and as on the date of the promulgation of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972, she was very much present in Bangladesh and her whereabouts were known to the Government, the case property cannot be treated as an abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2(1) of the said P.O.

14. Mr. T.H. Khan next submits that the oral gift was acted upon both by the donor and the donee and the Indian High Commission merely wanted some time to recognize the donee as its landlady after getting a nod from the Indian Government, but this was not appreciated by the Court of Settlement and as such there was a miscarriage of justice.

15. Mr. T.H. Khan also submits that from legalistic point of view, the petitioner is the landlady of the Indian High Commission and in this perspective, she is entitled to get monthly rent therefrom; but it has been illegally paying rent to the Government in respect of the case property as abandoned property.

15. Mr. T.H. Khan also submits that from legalistic point of view, the petitioner is the landlady of the Indian High Commission an in this perspective, she is entitled to get monthly rent therefrom; but it has been illegally paying rent to the Government in respect of the case property an abandoned property.

16. Mr. T.H. Khan has drawn our attention to the decision in the case of Bangladesh Appellant. Vs. Rehana Kamal and others Respondents reported in 56 DLR (AD) 1 in support of his contention that the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha has been managing the case property through her tenant, that is, the Indian High Commission and as such it cannot be said that she has not been occupying, supervising and/or managing the property through the tenant; but curiously enough, the court of Settlement lost sight of this aspect of the case causing a failure of justice.

17. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Abdul Kader Talukder, the learned Assistant Attorney-General (as he was then) appearing for the respondent Government and the RAJUK, submits that the alleged, oral gift dated 14.12.1970 under the Mohammedam Law in favour of the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha by the original owner Mrs. Atia Siddiqui is not valid in view of the fact that the petitioner did never get delivery of possession of the case property pursuant thereto and from this stand-point, the court below rightly rejected the prayer of the petitioner for its release from the 'Ka' list of abandoned properties

18. Mr. Md. Abdul Kader Talukder further submits that on the date of promulgation of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972, the owner of the case property, that is to say, Mrs. Atia Siddiqui was absent in this country and her whereabouts were not known to the Government, though she was in Pakistan and in such view of the matter, the case property was treated as an abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2(1) of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972 and that being so, no exception can be taken thereto.

19. Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate appearing for the added-respondent No. 3 in Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001, contends that the case property being an abandoned property along with other properties was put to auction sale by an auction notice published in "The Daily Janakantha' and in response to that notice, the added-respondent no. 3 submitted his bid and the bid being the highest was accepted by the RAJUK and accordingly, he deposited the lamest money to the tune of Tk. 25,00,000/- in the account of the RAJUK; but because of the stay-order passed in Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001, he could not deposit the balance amount of money and his fate is awaiting its adjudication.

20. Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmud further contends that the Court of Settlement appreciated the evidence and materials on record in their proper perspective and accordingly, it came to the finding that the alleged oral gift dated 14.12.1970 was not acted upon inasmuch as the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha did not get delivery of possession of the case property on the basis thereof.

21. By drawing our attention the decision in the case of the Government of Bangladesh Appellant Vs.  Asraf Ali and another Respondents reported in 2 MLR (AD)96, Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmud next submits that the enlistment of the case property as an abandoned property in the 'Ka' list has a presumptive value in la as to its correctness unless it is rebutted by adducing evidence to the contrary; but it transpires that the petitioner has failed to rebut the presumption of correctness attached to the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings by adducing evidence to the contrary and this being the scenario, the judgment and order of the lower Court is not liable to be interfered with.

22. Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmud also submits that while exercising the certiorari writ jurisdiction, the High Court Division cannot sit over the judgment of a Tribunal as a Court of Appeal Nad similarly it cannot decide the dispute which is based on facts by taking a different view from that of the Tribunal'. In support of this submission, he has relied upon the self-same decision reported in 2 MLR (AD)96 (supra).."

23. Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmud next contends that there is no onus on the Bangladesh Government to prove that the case property is an abandoned property; but the onus is squarely on the claimant of the property to prove that the property is not an abandoned property. In this connection, he has made a reference to the decision in the case of the Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh and another Appellants Vs. Rowshan Ara Begum and another Respondents reported in 57DLR(AD)167.

24. It is the definite assertion on the part of the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha that the oral gift dated 14.12.1972 was acted upon and she got constructive possession of the case property pursuant thereto and the Indian High Commission has been her tenant, though it has been paying monthly rent to the Government.

25. In this regard, a reference may be made to Annexure-C in Writ Petition No. 2603 of 2000, Annexure-C is a declaration of the oral gift dated 14.12.1970. From a plain reading of Annexure-C, it appears that the donee Mrs. Zakia Doha has been delivered possession of the case property by the donor and she (Mrs. Zakia Doha) being the donee is in full and complete possession of the same in her own right. Of course, Annexure-C does not indicate the nature of her possession, that is to say, whether physical or constructive in relation to the case property. Anyway, as per Annexure-C, she is in full and complete possession of the case property in her own right. But this assertion in Annexure-C does not appear to be in keeping with the materials on record. It appears that the gift of the case property along with the tenancy of the Indian High Commission was not made to the petitioner. In other words, we do not find any reference whatsoever to the tenancy of the Indian High Commission therein. We fail to understand why Annexure-C is conspicuously silent about the tenancy of the Indian High Commission.

<u>26. It is the definite claim of the petitioner that the oral gift of the case property was made in her favour on 14.12.1970. It is a truism that the War of Liberation started on 26th March 1971 and ended on 161 December, 1971. It seems that prior to commencement of the War of Liberation in 1971, she got more than 3 months time to enter into a fresh tenancy agreement with the Indian High Commission; but this having not been done by her; it is difficult for a man of ordinary prudence to hold that she got constructive possession of the case property on the basis of the oral gift dated 14.12.1970. It is undisputed that the Indian High Commission did not attorn her as its land lady, rather the High Commission has been paying monthly rent to the Government in respect of the case property as an abandoned property. The finding of the Court of Settlement that the possession of the case property was not delivered to the petitioner in pursuance of the alleged oral gift is hard to find fault with. This finding of the Court of Settlement is a factual finding and this finding cannot be knocked down under Article 102 of the Constitution by taking a different view on the question of the factual aspect of the matter (vide 2 MLR(AD)96).</u>

27. As already observed, the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha did not get delivery of possession, either physical or constructive, of the case property pursuant to the alleged oral gift dated 14.12.1970. It is an indubitable fact that 30 days' prior notice was not given by Mrs. Atia Siddiqui to the DIT and no prior transfer fee was paid thereto for transfer of the case property in favour of her sister Mrs. Zakia Doha as stipulated in Clause 23 of the deed of lease dated 08.06.1965. So this alleged transfer by way of gift is a flagrant contravention of Clause 23 of the said deed of lease. On this score, the RAJUK did not mutate the name of the petitioner in its records. Precisely speaking, the RAJUK did not recognize the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha as a transferee from her sister Mrs. Atia Siddiqui by way of gift.

28. The reliance of Mr. T.H. Khan on the decision in the case of Bangladesh Appellant Vs. Rehana Kamal and others Respondents reported in 56 DLR (AD)1 does not appear to be of any avail to him. In that case, the tenant American Embassy acknowledged the respondents as their landladies, paid rent to them and the tenancy agreement was renewed in 1973 and it has been paying rent regularly in their account with the American Express Bank in Dhaka. So it is ex-facie clear that the facts and circumstances of that case are quite distinguishable from those of the instant case.

29. The upshot of our above discussion that the oral gift dated 14.12.1972 was not acted upon because of non-delivery of possession of the case property, whether physical or constructive, in favour of the donee Mrs. Zakia Doha by the donor Mrs. Atia Siddiqui. As has been found by the Court of Settlement, on the date of promulgation of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and disposal) Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 16 of 1972), that is, on 28.02.1972, the owner Mrs. Atia Siddiqui was not available in Bangladesh, rather she was in Pakistan as a Pakistani citizen which was at war with or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh thus attracting the mischief of Article 2(1) of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972. Of course, at a subsequent stage, she settled down in Surrey, U.K.

<u>30. It is well-settled that the onus is upon the petitioner to prove that the case property is not an abandoned property. By the way, the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) may be adverted to. Sub-Section (2) of Section 5 of the Ordinance provides that the lists published under Sub-Section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned properties and have vested in the Government as such undeniably, Mrs. Atia Siddiqui is not the claimant of the case property. The alleged oral gift dated 14.12.1970 having not been acted upon, the petitioner also cannot be the claimant of the property in question. She is, so to say, a busy body with reference to the said property. What we are driving at is this: the petitioner has no locus standi to lay any claim thereto.</u>

<u>31. Section 7 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 enjoins the claimant before the Court of Settlement to prove that the property is not abandoned property, in a like manner a plaintiff is to prove his case and the Government, like that of a defendant, is under no legal obligation to prove that the property is an abandoned property or to disclose the basis of treating the property as an abandoned property as held, referring to some authorities, in the decision in the case of the Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh and another Appellants Vs. Rowshan Ara Begum and another Respondents reported in 57 DLR(AD) 167.</u>

32. Coming back to the decision in the case of the Government of Bangladesh Appellant Vs. Asraf Ali and another Respondents reported in 2 MLR (AD) 96 referred to by Mr. Rokon Uddin Mahmud, we find in paragraph 8:

"8. It has been held by this Division in various decisions that the enlistment of a building under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 raises a presumption in law that the property is an abandoned property under Section 5(2) of the Ordinance. This presumption is, of course, a rebuttable presumption; but the respondent No. 1 failed to rebut this presumption. No rebuttable evidence could be adduced to show that the original owner Yahiya was present in Bangladesh and he occupied, managed or supervised the disputed building when the P.O. No. 16 of 1972 came into operation. Hence the listing of the property as an abandoned property in the Supplementary. Provisions Ordinance, 1985 was lawful as it was an abandoned property by operation of law".

33. To our mind, the above principle that has been enunciated in that decision applies aptly the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

34. It transpires that the Court of Settlement has made a finding as to non-passing of title of the petitioner to the case property. In a case before the Court of Settlement, it is the duty of the court to decide the character of the property, whether abandoned or not. While deciding the character of the property, it may refer to the prima facie title or otherwise of the petitioner. But the question of title cannot be conclusively decided in a case before the Court of Settlement as it is done in a civil suit before the Civil Court. This finding about the non-passing of title to the petitioner with reference to the case property is definitely un-tenable in law. But none the less, the finding will not detract from the treatment of the case property as an abandoned property by operation of law.

35. In a last-ditch attempt, Mr. T.H. Khan has argued that the Government did not take over possession of the case property prior to its inclusion in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23.09.1986 and as such its enlistment as an abandoned is without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

36. There is nothing on record to show that the petitioner has taken any plea or stand as regards not taking over possession of the case property by the Government before its inclusion in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings either in the application made before the Court of Settlement under Section 7(1) of the. Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 or in the Writ Petition Na 2603 of 2000. Furthermore, it is well-settled that the Government is not under any legal obligation to disclose the basis for treatment of the case property as an abandoned property. This being the state of affairs, the above argument of Mr. T.H. Khan stands negative.

37. It appears that the petitioner Mrs. Zakia Doha has been in Bangladesh all through. Her presence in the country has not been denied or disputed by any quarter. But as the alleged oral gift dated 14.12.1970 has fallen to the ground, we are not concerned with her presence or otherwise in this country on the date of promulgation of the P.O. No. 16 of 1972, that is, on 28.02.1972.

38. As to the Writ Petition No. 5721 of 1997, nobody has appeared before us in support of the Rule issued therein at the instance of one Mrs. Atia Siddiqui. Since nobody has turned up to conduct the hearing of the Rule issued in that Writ Petition, it is liable to be discharged for default; albeit Mr. Md. Abdul Kader Talukder is before us on behalf of the respondent No. 1-Government.

39. From the foregoing discussions and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, we find no merit in the Rules issued in Writ Petition no. 2603 of 2000 and Writ Petition No. 1042 of 2001 and accordingly, the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. In Writ Petition No. 5721 of 1997, the Rule is discharged for default without any order as to costs.

40. Let the lower Court records along with a copy of this judgment be sent down at once,

End.

full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 01.09.2009 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 04 of 2009 affirming those dated 22.02.2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No. 09 of 2000 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus the present petitioners as pre-emptors tiled a pre-emption Miscellaneous Case in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, Barisal being Miscellaneous Case No. 09 of 2000 under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, contending inter alia that the case land originally belonged to one Tulshi Lal Banik.  The opposite party No.1 was a monthly tenant\under the pre-emptors and other co-sharers of the case land. On 15.03.2000 A.D. the pre-emptors while demanded arrear of rent of the premises the pre-emptee-opposite party No.1 disclosed that he has purchased 4 annas share of the land from the opposite party No.2. Thereafter, having obtained the certified copy of the kabla deed the pre-emptors finally came to learn that the vendor-opposite party no.2 transferred the case land in favour of the opposite party no.1 by a registered sub-kabla deed dated 19.01.1999 A.D. The kabla deed was registered on 28.12.1999 A.D. The petitioners being co-sharers of the land of S.A. khatian No. 20 are entitled to pre-empt the case land which is urgently required by them and as a result for getting the land pre-empted the pre-emptor-appellant-petitioners instituted the original miscellaneous case.

3. Vis-a-vis; the contrary case of the contesting opposite party Nos. 1(ka)-1(Cha) in short is thus that the case is barred by limitation and the case holding relating to the land of case kabla having been separated on an application filed, from the side of the pre-emptors' father the pre-emptors are seized to be the co-sharers of the case land and as such they are not entitled to pre-empt the case land. The further case of the opposite parties is such that the pre-emptor's father opened different khatians by mutation cases and paid rent separately during his life time and that's why the pre-emptors had no locustandi.

4. The learned trial court by his judgment and order dated 22.02.2009 dismissed the pre-emption miscellaneous case and being aggrieved the pre-emptors preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 04 of 2009 in the court of learned District Judge, Barisal and the learned appellate court by the impugned judgment and order dated 01.09.2009 dismissed the miscellaneous appeal affirming the judgment and order of the trial court.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the pre-emptor-appellant-petitioners have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

6. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. Tapan Kumar Chokraborty the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner's submits that the learned trial court as well as the appellate court committed illegality in dismissing the original case and its subsequent appeal. Only for one reason the pre-emption miscellaneous case was dismissed, which is 'separation of jama'. The original S.A. khatian no. 20 corresponding to the case land has been separated on 22.09.1991, but no court considered that the mutation case by dint of which the 'jama' was separated has been set aside subsequently in Miscellaneous case No. 29 K.T./99-2000 vide exhibit-`ga'. The learned Advocate further submits that the order of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Barisal has been submitted before the learned appellate court for taking notice as additional evidence but the appellate court without considering the papers passed the impugned judgment and order illegally. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the order dated 29.03.2000 passed by the concerned Assistant Commissioner (Land), Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No. 25 K.T./1999-2000 canceling the Sub-division khatian Nos. 554 and 698 was considered by the learned appellate court and from the order of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Barisal it is apparent that the Sub-division khatian No. 554 and 698 have no existence and the original holding of the S.A. khatian No. 20 remained intact and the pre-emptors as such remained co-sharers to the original holding.

8. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioners the teamed Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the submissions advanced from the side of the pre-emptor-petitioners and submits that it is the concurrent findings of both the courts below that the pre-emptor-petitioners are seized to be the co-sharers of the case land which was transferred in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite parties. The case kabla was registered on 28.12.1999 under section 60 of the Registration Act and the case holding was separated on 21.09.1991 at the instance of the father of the pre-emptors namely Narayon Chandra Banik. The vendor of the case land separated the juma in his name on 03.08.1999 and thereafter executed the case kabla in favour of the vendee. Admittedly; the original S.A. khatian is 20 and the mutation khatian is 554. This mutation khatian no 554 stands recorded in the name of the pre-emptor-petitioner's father vide exhibit-kha. Within the content of the case kabla (exhibit-ka) there is a recital that the father of the pre-emptors and the vendor of the ease kabla opened separate khatians. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate court not considered the subsequent cancellation of the mutation case as alleged from the side of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is not correct. The correct proposition is such that both the courts below considering the facts and circumstances of the case held that the act of cancellation is mulafide which is 'after thought' for the very purpose of the pre-emption miscellaneous case. The learned Advocate also submits that the exhibited documents especially; exhibit-`ka' goes to show that after the death of the pre-emptor's father in imitation case No. 432(1K.T.)/1995-96 the petitioners has opened separate khatian pursuant to previous mutation case No. 554. Thereafter, at the instance of one Meghnath Paul an application under section 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was filed on 29.03.2000 for amalgamation of the holding after cancellation of all previous mutation on the ground that no notice was served upon the co-sharers. It further appears that on the same date i.e. on 29.03.2000 without serving notice the order of amalgamation was given by the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Barisal. The learned Advocate submits that under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 service of notice is a pre-condition of the order of amalgamation of holding. But the fact remains that no notice was served upon the co-sharers of the land. In this context; the learned Advocate referred a decision of our Apex Court reported in 37 DLR(AD)212. The Advocate lastly submits that both the courts below in their observation and findings concurrently held that the order of amalgamation would not help the pre-emptor-petitioners as because the kabla deed against which the pre-emption miscellaneous ease was instituted is prior to the amalgamation of the holding and with a malice subsequently the order of amalgamation was obtained for the very purpose of the miscellaneous case for getting the land pre-empted. There is no such illegality or irregularity or misreading and non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and order can be interfered with.

9. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case record, exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses and other connected papers.

<u>10. On perusal of the case records it transpires that the case kabla against which the pre-emption-miscellaneous case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 has been filed was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 28.12.1999 and it is the observation of the appellate court in consultation with the relevant papers on records that at the time of case kabla there was no existence of the order of amalgamation.</u>

<u>11. Scrutinizing the evidence on record it appears that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Barisal vide his order dated 29.03.2000 passed the order of amalgamation pursuant to a miscellaneous case being No. 25 K.T./1999-2000 and after that the jama of the holding was separated and subsequent to that new khatian was opened.</u>

<u>12. In the case of Md. Abdur Rouf and others -vs.- Ahmeda Khatun and others, reported in 33 DLR(AD)323 our Apex Court in connection with the provisions laid down in section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act held that in a mutation case of split up of a jam; notice of the mutation case not having been served on the co-sharers and mutation having been effected behind their back, is not valid in law and the splitting up of the jama have no legal effect. Sub-division as well as consolidation (amalgamation) of a joint tenancy can only be effected after service of notice on the co-sharers vide the case law reported in 35 DLR(AD)338.</u>

13. Consulting the relevant papers on records in the instant case I have come across that for amalgamation of the jama one Meghnath Paul Chowdhury filed an application under section 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for review of the order of mutation passed earlier by the concerned revenue officer which was initiated at the instance of the petitioner's predecessor-in-interest one Narayan Chandra Banik on 29.03.2000. For amalgamation of the holding after cancellation of all previous mutation the proceeding was started and behind the back of other co-sharers in that proceeding on the same date without service of notice the Revenue Officer passed an order of amalgamation after cancellation of all previous mutation; which is obviously malafide and fraud.

14. During hearing of this revisional application the learned counsel on behalf of the petitioners has drawn my attention on ground No. 1 of the revisional application wherein it is cited that the learned District Judge i.e. the lower appellate court committed error of law in not considering that the sub-division of the holding relating to the original S.A. khatian is no more in existence and as such the teamed lower appellate court committed illegality ignoring that the sub-division khatian Nos. 554 and 698 are not in existence at present and the original holding of the S.A. khatian No. 20 remain intact, In this regard; having gone through the impugned judgment and order I have every reason to differ with the learned Advocate Mr. Quayum inasmuch as the learned lower appellate court consulting the relevant papers and evidence on records agreed with the learned Advocate appearing from the side of the respondents therein that the order of amalgamation will not help the appellants since the execution and registration of the case kabla was completed earlier and at the time of registration of the deed there was no existence of the order of amalgamation. It is the observation and decisions of both the courts below that the holding stands separated under the law. It is a fact that the separation of tenancy/jama khatian disentitles the pre-emptors from the right of pre-emption as the status of co-sharership in a tenancy of non-agricultural and ceases through two different ways: One is partition of land and the other is separation of the tenancy by splitting up the jama khatian; as the instant case be. Here in this case the factual aspect is such that, pursuant to mutation case No. 191 K.T./1991- 1992 a new Khatian was opened which is khatian No. 554 in the name of the predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptor-petitioners vide exhibit-ka'. In order to get an order of pre-emption the petitioners must be co-sharers of the holding and if it is found that at the time of transfer the petitioners are not the co-sharers in the case holding and a new khatian is opened in that case the petitioners cannot be legally entitled to get the pre-emption as sought for.

15. In view of the submissions of the learned Advocates scrutinizing the pleadings of the parties as well as the evidence on records I have the reason to draw such inference that the submission advanced from the side of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties is consistent and it deserve consensus of this Court. In this case inasmuch as save and except the matter in issue on the locus standi of the pre-emptor-petitioners the other points are not agitated from any comer I find nothing to hold such a view that the courts below in deciding the points for determination as recorded committed any error of law. There is no such misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and order can be interfered with under the ambit of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

16. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and discussions referred to above I am constrained to hold such a view that the Rule have got no substance to succeed.

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 01.09.2009 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 04 of 2009 affirming those dated 22.02.2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court, Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No. 09 of 2000 is hereby affirmed.

18. Communicate the judgment and order at once and send back the lower Court's record immediately.

End.
