full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J. This appeal arises from First Appeal No. 27 of 1981 affirming the judgment and decree in Money Suit No. 172 of 1974 passed by the Subordinate Judge of 3rd Court, Dhaka on September 30, 1980.

2. Facts as stated in the plaint show that on November 29, 1974 plaintiff-respondent No. 1 Sonali Bank, (which I will call "The Bank") instituted the suit against the appellant. M.M. Ispahani Ltd. (which I will call "The Company"), and respondent Nos. 2-6 for recovery of the debt along with accrued interest amounting to Tk. 3, 49, 14, 738,70. Appellant as principal debtor obtained the loan from the National Bank of Pakistan under the cash credit limit of Taka 4 crores and overdraft limit of Taka 33 lacs against the security of demand promissory notes, hypothecation of jute stored at various purchase centres, pledge of shares of different Companies, charges on the Company's book debts and assets and stocks in trade owned by the appellant company personal guarantees of the directors of the appellant company which made them personally liable. Sonali Bank which is the successor of the National Bank of Pakistan was created by the President's Order No. 26 of 1972, (The Bangladesh Banks (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 vesting all the assets; rights and interest subsisting in the National Bank of Pakistan within the territory of Bangladesh.

3. After the emergence of Bangladesh as a separate Stale the appellant company was taken over by the Government under the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972. On February 2, 1972 respondent No. 7 was appointed an administrator of the appellant company under the provisions of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. He took over the entire stock of jute available in the aforesaid godowns of the appellant's company. As the appellant company did not repay the loan, total dues of the Bank in cash credit account and overdraft account stood at Tk. 3,49,14,738.70 on November 29, 1974; the date of the filing of the suit.

4. On February 7, 1977 the appellant company filed written statement. Respondent Nos. 2-6 who are the directors of the company and guarantors for the repayment of the debt did neither appear in the suit nor file any written statement. In the written statement filed by the appellants company it was stated inter alia, that:

"(a) the suit is not maintainable.

(b) the suit is barred under the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972.

(c) the suit is bad for non-joinder of Government of Bangladesh and Jute Corporation as parties.

(d) respondent No. 1 is not the successor-in-interest of National Bank of Pakistan and cannot claim the debt.

(e) the Administrator recklessly dealt with the assets and stock of the appellant. The hypothecated stocks were always sufficient to the advances actually made from time to time and after Administrator was appointed proper evaluation of the hypothecated stocks were never made with notice to the directors of the appellant and any collusive and incorrect evaluation cannot bind the appellant.

(f) the statements of the plaint regarding interest at the rates and for the period as alleged in the plaint and the liability to pay Tk. 3,49.14,738.70 were denied."

The suit was decreed exparte on 28-4-78. But on an appeal filed by the appellant company it was restored for hearing on October 9, 1980.

5. At the hearing of the suit, it appears that the appellant company's principal defence, among others, was that the Sonali Bank was not legally entitled to recover the debt payable to the National Bank of Pakistan as it had not taken over all the assets and liabilities of that Bank. In short, its claim to be the successor-in-interest of the National Bank of Pakistan was untenable. Further, the company along with the jute stocks and other assets and liabilities was taken over by the Government, the liability to repay the loan also passed to it.

6. The trial court, on considering the provisions of Presidents Order No. 26 of 1972 held that the Sonali Bank was the successor-in-interest of the National Bank of Pakistan and therefore had, the right of recovery of the debt owing to that Bank. After considering the evidence and materials on record in further held that the suit was not barred by limitation and also not bad for non-joinder of the Government and the Jute Corporation.

7. Accordingly the trial court passed a decree for Tk. 6,31,10,307.13 with interest thereon at the rate of 12% per annum till realisation.

8. Appellant company preferred first Appeal No 27 of 1981 in the High Court Division. Responder Nos. 2-6 did not file any appeal. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court Division. The learned Judges expressed their reluctance to allow addition grounds to be urged before them. Moreover of scrutinizing the grounds the learned Judges of the High Court Division found them to be without any substance.

9. In rejecting the contention of the appellant company that as neither the Government nor the Jute Marketing Corporation was impleaded in the suit it was not maintainable. The learned Judges the High Court Division observed as follows:

‘‘From the facts disclosed in the case it is clear that the management and control of defendant No. 1 including its Jute Division had been fully resumed by the Directors the Company by October 1976.

10. So far as the rate of interest upto the date of filing the suit was concerned the Hi, Court Division relying on the case of Harid Ranchordas V. Mercantile Bank of India Ltd. 47 ILR Bom. 474 held that the Rule of interest which was charged by the Bank was applicable as no objection was raised by the appellant and as it was duly shown in the statements of accounts on the basis of which entries were made therein. As to the rate of interest from the date of the filing of the suit to the date of judgment the High Court Division held that as the award of interest fell within the discretion of the Court which was duly exercised by it no interference was called for. The Order of interest at the rate of 12% during the pendency of the suit and until realisation did not suffer from any illegality. Reliance was placed on two judgments of the Privy Council namely Panna Lal V. Nihai Chand AIR 1922 PC 46 and Lala Hakim Rai V. Lala Ganga Ram : AIR 1942 PC 61.

11. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court Division the appellant company moved this Court. Leave was granted to consider the following contentions of the learned Counsel for the appellant company:

"(a) That the High Court Division erroneously came to the conclusion that the control and management of the Jute Division was fully resumed by the Directors of the petitioner company and failed to pursue the legal aspects of the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972 read with Ordinance No. XX of 1975 and Ordinance No. XLIX of 1976:

(b) That the Bangladesh Jute Marketing Corporation was a necessary party and the courts below were wrong in not dismissing the suit for not impleading the necessary parties; and

(c) That the contract between the petitioner and the former National Bank of Pakistan having been superseded by Law the right of creditor and the obligation of the debtor having merged in the same hand i.e. Government of Bangladesh, the liability of the petitioner had become extinct and as such, the said liability was not enforceable against the petitioner."

12. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed. Counsel for the appellant company, while referring to the provisions of several enactments, namely, P.O. 16 of 1972. P.O. 26/72. Ordinance No. XX of 1975 and Ordinance No. XLIX of 1976, sought to establish that the assets and properties which were offered as security for obtaining the loan were taken over by the Government and it also took over the management and control of Ispahani Group of Industries. The Government also appointed an administrator for them who was authorised to conduct their affairs including operation of bank accounts. Though some of the concerns of the appellant company were subsequently released, business and the assets of the Jute Division of the appellant company remained vested in the Jute Marketing Corporation.

13. The learned Counsel submitted that since the Government took over all the assets and properties of the appellant company including the jute stocks in the three godowns mentioned above which were hypothecated with the Bank for the satisfaction and discharge of the loan in case of the appellant's inability to repay according to the stipulations in the loan agreement, it is the Government which is liable for the company's debts along with interest if any. The appellant company can under no circumstances, be said to be under any obligation to repay the loan. It appears that Ispahani Group of Industries was taken over by the Government under Government Notification dated 26th January. 1972 under the provisions of Acting President's Order dated 30th December 1971. When President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated, the same vested in the Government under its provisions. From the provisions of Ordinance No. XX of 1975 it appears that there is a mention of Jute Division of the appellant company which includes Zareen Jute Baling Industries. Khulna industries Ltd. and Keraniganj Jute Baling Company Limited all of which are transferred to the Bangladesh Jute Corporation. The provisions were inserted under new Section 25A of the Bangladesh Jute Corporation. 1973.

14. Appellant's Counsel stressed hard on the retention of the Jute Division of the appellant company by the Jute Corporation which, according to his showing, was never released in favour of the appellant company. He submitted that the Jute Division which was taken over by the Government in 1971 including the entire jute stocks which were offered as security against the present loan and remained with the Jute Corporation. He referred to two Government Notifications dated 18-6-74 and 19-6-74 (Vide Ext.E and E(1), Under these notifications concerns of Ispahani Group of Industries other than the Jute Division of the appellant company were it appears released. The assets and liabilities of M.M. Ispahani Limited (Jute Division) were sub-sequently transferred to the Jute Marketing Corporation by the Promulgation of Ordinance No. XLIX of 1976. Under its provisions the Jute Corporation to which the assets and liabilities of M.M. Ispahani Ltd. Jute Division, were transferred earlier under Ordinance No. XX of 1975 was abolished. The provisions of Section (2) of this Ordinance provides as follows :-

"(2) Upon the repeal of the said Act-

(a) all assets, rights powers authorities and privileges, and all property, movable and immovable, cash and bank balance, funds, investments and all other rights and interests in or arising out of, such property, and all books of accounts, registers, records and documents, of the Bangladesh Jute Corporation, hereinafter referred to as the Jute Corporation shall stand transferred to and vest in, the Bangladesh Jute Marketing Corporation Act, 1957 (E.P. Act XII of 1957), hereinafter referred to as the Jute Marketing Corporation.

(b) all debts and liabilities in obligations undertaken, all contracts entered into and all agreements, made by or with the Jute Corporation and subsisting or having effect immediately before such repeal shall be deemed to have been incurred, undertaken, entered into or made by or with the Jute Marketing Corporation;

(c) all Officers and other employees of the Jute Corporation shall stand transferred to and become officers and employees of the Jute Marketing Corporation and shall hold office or service in the Jute Marketing Corporation on the same terms and conditions as were enjoyed by them immediately before such repeal and shall continue to do so until these terms and conditions are altered by the Government or by the Jute Marketing Corporation.

Provided that no officer or other employee whose services are so transferred shall be entitled to any compensation because of such transfer;

(d) all suits and other legal proceedings instituted by or against the Jute Corporation before such repeal shall be deemed to be suits and proceeding by or against the Jute Marketing Corporation and shall be proceeded or otherwise dealt with accordingly."

15. Referring to the deed of Agreement between the Bangladesh Jute Marketing Corporation and M.M. Ispahani Ltd. dated 19th October, 1976 (vide. Ext.G). the learned Counsel for the appellant tried to assert that though Zareen Jute Baling Company Limited, Khulna Industries Ltd. and Keraniganj Jute Baling Company Limited were transferred back to the appellant company the Jute Marketing. Corporation did not release the business and assets of the Jute Division of the appellant company.

16. Incidentally, it may briefly be mentioned here that there is no reference of the Jute Division or its release anywhere in the Agreement, whether in the recital portion or the operative part of the Agreement itself. We shall consider this agreement later in this judgment. Suffice it to say, if there was such vital connection between the loan agreement and the Jute Division of the appellant company which finds reference in the two Ordinances and the Agreement referred to above, it is surprising to sec why this omission has occurred.

17. The main trend of the Counsel's argument seemed to veer round the Government's taking over the jute business of the appellant company along with its jute stocks which were offered as security for the repayment of the loan. Mr. Ahmed quite vehemently asserted that when the Government of the country took over the entire Ispahani Group of Industries including the properties hypothecated to the predecessor of the Sonali Bank, respondent No. I, against which the appellant company had no remedy, respondent No. 1 should have, in all fairness, proceeded against the Government. Liability to repay the loan is inseparable from the assets against which the loan was obtained. Since the assets against which the loans were advanced passing over to the Government, the liability to repay which attached to it also passed to the Government. The appellant company must be considered to have been released of its obligation to repay. Appellant's Counsel, while referring to the Government which appointed an Administrator and the subsequent transfer of the company's assets and liabilities to the Jute Corporation and Jute Marketing Corporation successively, submitted that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of either the Government or the Jute Marketing Corporation who as it appears, were not impleaded in the suit by the respondent bank. According to him, therefore, the suit was bad for non-joinder of necessary parties and liable to be dismissed.

18. In this connection the learned Counsel further submitted that the recovery of the loan amount from the appellant-company was to he in accordance with the loan agreement between it and the bank. But since the property covered by the agreement vested in the Government" as abandoned property under the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972, the agreement could only be enforced after complying with Article 9 of the aforesaid Order . Provisions of this Article require the determination of liability when any property is taken over by the Government as abandoned property. In the present case whether such determination has at all been made by the Government in accordance with the Rules made under the Order cannot be decided in the absence of the Government as a necessary party.

19. Finally, appellant's Counsel contended that in view of the plaintiff-respondent's claim of Tk. 3,49,14,738.70 the decree for realisation of Tk. 6,31,10,307.13 us confirmed by the High Court Division cannot stand. Further, the Order of interest in disregard of the provision of Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not justified.

20. Dr. Kamal Hossain, Counsel for the respondent bank, before making his submissions on the points raised by the appellant's Counsel, pointedly referred to the slow and meandering course of the defence adopted by the appellant-company. There was inordinate delay in filing the written statement. Submissions made before the courts find no basis in it. Further, the appellant company is seen to constantly change its position, both regarding facts and Law. Thus, before the trial Court the appellant company, according to him, tried to defeat the Bank's claim by denying the debtor-creditor relationship, for, the appellant company considered that since the National Bank of Pakistan from which it had taken the loan still existed it was not liable to make the repayments to the Sonali Bank. This position was according to Dr. Hossain given up by the appellant company during the hearing of the appeal before the High Court Division where its stand was that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of the Government and the Jute Corporation or Jute Marketing Corporation as they are necessary parties. Still, the appellant company has made further departure from its positions adopted in the courts below by making submissions on newer grounds before this Court. The reason for this ever-changing claims is that the appellant company knowing fully well that it was not in a position to deny its liability for the amount covered by the agreement concerned resorted to newer grounds at every stage of the proceedings.

21. Next. Dr. Kamal Hossain mentioned that there is no plausible explanation as to why the appellant company did not file any written statement for very long and allowed the suit to be decreed exparte and then filed an application for restoration of the suit. Further, no explanation has been offered as to why the other respondent Nos. 2-6 who are the guarantors and liable for repaying the loan did not file any written statement at all nor contested the suit, nor did they file any appeal either before the High Court Division or even before this Court.

22. As no argument was advanced before us by the appellant's Counsel as to whether the Sonali Bank succeeded to the assets and liabilities of the National Bank of Pakistan Limited, there was no corresponding necessity for the respondent's Counsel to make any submissions on the point of succession. Still the respondent's Counsel mentioned that from the provisions of P.O. 26 of 1972 it would appear that the Sonali Bank succeeded to the assets and liabilities of the National Bank of Pakistan Limited as existed within the territory of Bangladesh.

23. Dr. Hossain submitted that so far as the loan is concerned. Mirza Mehedy Ispaham. D.W. No. 1 who was Chairman of the Board of Directors of the appellant company admitted its liability to the National Bank of Pakistan minus Taka 99 lacs which were deposited in the loan account including interest stood at Tk. 3,49,14,738.70 only. (on the date of filing the suit). On its application the National Bank of Pakistan allowed the appellant company a cash credit limit of Taka 4 crores and also a secured over draft limit of Taka 33 lacs on 12-9-69 in renewal and continuation of the previous loan.

24. Terms and conditions of the cash credit limit were as follows;

"1. Demand promissory note;

2. Hypothecation of jute stocks (baled and loose) stored at various purchasing and baling centres, and jute in transit throughout the then East Pakistan;

3. Pledge of shares;

4. Personal guarantee by all the Directors of the company, namely, respondent Nos. 2-6:

5. Hypothecation of book debts and assets."

25. As to the liability to repay the outstanding amount of the loan, Dr. Kamal Hossain submitted that this is recoverable from the appellant-company and the aforesaid Directors who furnished personal guarantees. The priority of the choices to seek repayment from either the company or its Director's rested with the creditor bank in whose favour the decree stands.

<u>26. In elaborating the extent of the liability of the guarantor to repay the loan, Dr. Hossain, went on to say that the liability is in no way dependent upon the principal debtor namely the appellant company. Without even suing the principal debtor for the repayment of the loan or before proceeding to execute the decree for its repayment the creditor may-seek to proceed against the guarantors or execute the decree against them. Reliance was placed on the decision of Indian Supreme Court in the Bank of Hibar Ltd. V. Damodar Prasad. : AIR 1969 SC 297. For the proposition that a guarantor is liable to pay even where the creditor omits to sue the principal debtor the guarantor's liability is not deferred until the creditor exhausts his remedies against the principal debtor. His liability is immediate. Further he has no right to restrain execution against him until the creditor has exhausted its remedies against the principal debtor. Again, in a Privy Council decision, namely Mahanth Singh V. U Ba Yi : AIR 1939 PC 11, where the creditor's claim to sue the principal debtor became barred by limitation, it was held that the guarantor was liable to pay. For the proposition that a creditor is not bound to resort to securities furnished by the principal debtor before suing the guarantor, the learned Counsel before suing the guarantor, the learned Counsel referred to Paget's Law of Banking (9th edition, 1982 p. 525) and Milnes Holden's Law and Practice of banking. Securities for Bankers (Vol. 2, Sixth edition, 1980 p. 266). On the basis of certain decisions it has been observed that where securities charged by borrower are sold by a creditor bank, a guarantor has no claim against the bank with regard to any alleged negligent disposal of the security and that the bank owed no duty to the guarantor to take reasonable care and skill to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable.</u>

27. Dr. Hossain then referred to the letters of guarantee furnished by respondent Nos. 2-6 for determining the independent nature of the liability irrespective of whether the liability against the appellant company, which is the principal debtor in the instant case is enforceable or not. If necessary, the conditions of the guarantee will, in due course, be referred to in the judgment.

28. As in the case of the guarantors position with regard to their liability to repay the loan, Dr. Hossain proceeded to show from the deed of hypothecation of the jute stocks that whether the appellant company suffered any disability or not due to external circumstances, its liability to repay the loan remained unaffected. The learned Counsel submitted that the hypothecation of jute stocks was only one of the five securities offered by the appellant company. From the deed of hypothecation, it appears that jute stocks remained in the possession of the appellant company. The bank was entitled to only the sale proceeds. Whether the jute stocks were disposed of by the appellant company or the administrator or the Corporation, the bank was not in any way responsible for the manner of their disposal. While referring to its definition as "a legal transaction whereby goods may be made available as security for a debt without transferring either the property or the possession to the creditor", Vide, Milnes Holden, Law and Practice of Banking : Securities for Bankers' Advances, Vol 2, (Sixth edition, 1980) para 24.1, p. 311, the learned Counsel submitted that the bank was under no duty to sell the jute stocks according to the terms of the deed of hypothecation, though the bank was given the power to sell them. In support, the learned Counsel also referred to the case of F. Nanak Chand Ramkishan Das V. Lal Chand Ganeshi Lal, reported in AIR 1958 Punj. 222.

29. If, therefore, the bank did not lay any claim to sell the jute stocks which passed to the Government on taking over the appellant company it cannot be held liable. The jute stocks in question were always in possession of the appellant company before it was taken over and remained with the administrator after he was put in-charge of the management of the appellant company's godowns. The learned Counsel expressed the view that the company being in possession of the jute stocks since the date of the' hypothecation it must be liable to the bank for their preservation and disposal. The bank is in no way concerned whether the jute stocks were destroyed or damaged or removed while they were in possession of the company or even if they were wasted or not accounted for by the administrator after the taking over.

30. Dr. Hossain also tried to maintain the correctness of the quantity of jute stocks declared to have been received by the administrator. He submitted that the appellant company did not have any greater quantity of jute in its possession at the time of taking over by the administrator. He doubted the accuracy of the statements of jute stocks, Ext. B series. His reasons for saying so are that it was not possible to provide such daily summary of jute stocks statements after December 13, 1971. The statements do not show any specific quantity of jute or of what quality or where such quantities where located and the summary statements, have not therefore, any factual basis. Apart from this summary statements the appellant company did not produce any other evidence to show the actual quantity of jute stocks after December 13, 1971. Had there been one lac fifty thousand bales of jute equivalent to eight lacs maunds in the stocks of the appellant company as claimed by it, the company would have taken insurance policies to cover the same. The company took only two insurance policies which were in force for the period ending December 24, 1971 covering Taka 60 lacs plus Taka 40 lacs. The 3rd insurance policy which was for Taka 1 crore 15 lacs expired on November 27, 1971.

31. Had the company raised the point in the trial court regarding the quantity of jute stocks as it now claims to have been in its possession at the time of taking over the bank would have produced evidence to show that it had not more than 40 thousand bales and also the prevailing market price for which also no evidence was given by the company at the trial of the suit. Further, no controversy was raised by the company regarding the quantity of jute stocks or the price at which the administrator sold the jute either in its correspondences between 1974 to 1976 nor when it took back the management of the concerns from the jute corporation in 1976. On the other hand, the company gave the undertaking to the Government to indemnify it if there was any counter claim against the Government by the company or any other person, Ext. F.

32. As regards the points raised by the appellant's Counsel, that since the Jute Division of the appellant company was not yet released the Company was not under any obligation to repay the loan as claimed by the bank the learned Counsel for the bank submitted that the company's grievances now being ventilated before this Court as to the retention of the Jute Division by the Government and the refusal to repay the loan on that ground were neither stated in the written statement nor taken before the courts below.

33. For the first time this grievance is being raised before this Court. When a person contracts a loan from a banking institution by offering valuable security but retaining its possession with itself, it cannot possibly lie in its mouth to deny the liability to repay the loan on the ground that the security has been lost, or destroyed or taken away by somebody by force or it had parted with its possession under compulsion.

58. For such loss or taking away of the security persons or bodies who are responsible for it may be liable, but can it be said that such plea is sufficient to absolve the person or body contracting the loan from his or its obligation to repay the loan. However specious the argument may seem to be on careful analysis of the situation it loses its attractiveness. It, therefore, follows that the company cannot succeed in avoiding the repayment of the loan to the respondent Bank.

59. So far as the non-impleading of the Jute Corporation or Jute Marketing Corporation or the Government is concerned the above conclusion regarding the subsistence of the appellant company's liability to repay the loan to the Bank negatives the necessity of making any one of them party in the suit. The relationship of creditor and debtor does not admit of the introduction of any other person in a suit filed by one against the other, for determining their relationship as such creditor or debtor in respect of a loan transaction, unless such other person or persons are in any way formally connected with it, by formally according to share any obligation arising from such loan. To my mind it seems that only a guarantor or a co-mortgagor or assignee of the debtor's interest or liability may be made a party to such suit. As the company including the three subsidiary companies has already been returned, the question before us is not as to what would have been the position if the company including the three subsidiary companies were not released by the Government, but the question is whether after the release the company is still liable for its debts previous to the taking over by the Government. From the foregoing discussion it appears that the company must be held responsible for the repayment of the loan excluding what has already been paid to the Bank.

So far it appears that after the appointment of the administrator the amount of Taka 99 lacs was credited in the cash credit account of the company on November 23, 1972. This amount is to be deducted from the amount claimed to have been outstanding on December 13, 1971.

61. Whatever liability the Government or Jute Corporation or Jute Marketing Corporation may have incurred in respect of the loan under consideration cannot be determined in this suit. It would, therefore, be seen that none of them is a necessary party in the suit which is not liable to be dismissed on this ground. It is also not necessary to send the case back for impleading them.

<u>62. As regards the liability of the guarantors to repay the loan, the contention of Dr. Kamal Hossain appears to have judicial support from the decisions cited by him which show that the guarantor is seen not only responsible for repayment of the loan his liability to repay need not even be postponed till the principal debtor fails to repay the loan. From the priority point of view in repaying the loan, the guarantor may be compelled before even compelling the principal debtor to repay. The choice lies with the creditor. There is nothing in the deed of guaranty to show that respondents No. 2-6 have been absolved from repaying the loan unless the appellant company repaid the loan nor is there any clause therein postponing the priority in repaying the loan in their favour. There is also no explanation as to why the guarantors though served with notice did not appear either before the trial court nor preferred any appeal against the decree before the High Court Division. They did not also appear before us.</u>

63. What led them not to appear before the courts and put up defence, if any, such nonappearance does not certainly strengthen the position either of themselves or of the company. They are equally liable to repay the loan under consideration and so far as the priority in repaying is concerned it is for the respondent Bank to choose whether it will proceed against them first or the company in the matter of realising their outstanding dues.

64. The other question requires to be settled is the claim to interest on the principal debt.

65. We have heard the contentions of the learned Counsels of the appellant company and the respondent Bank regarding the award of interest. We have no hesitation in accepting the contention of the learned Counsel of the respondent Bank that the interest claimed upto 13-12-71 which we accepted as the date of acceptance of liability by the company must be at the contracted rate. If we had agreed this date to be the date of filing the suit, there would have been no valid reason for us not to concede to the argument of the learned Counsel for the respondent Bank, that is, to award interest at the contracted rate upto the date of filing the suit.

66. The reason for this is that upto 13-12-71 no objection appears to have been raised by the appellant company as to calculation of interest at the rate contracted by the parties and the entries made in the statement of accounts on the basis of such calculation. There is judicial support available in favour of this view. Thus, in the case of Haridas Ranchordas V. Mercantile Bank of India, ILR 44 Bom. 474 PC at pp. 480-481, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council observed as follows:

The pass book of the defendants with the Bank clearly shows that was the way in which interest was computed and charged in their account with the Bank. The defendants never, until after the 1st August. 1914 raised any objection to the principle of charging compound interest or to compound interest being charged by the Bank on their overdrafts. It was this course of business to which it must be taken that the defendants agreed. As long ago as 1813 Lord Ellenborough in Bruce V Hunter held that the fact that the defendant had not objected to a charge of compound interest in accounts which for several years he had annually received from the plaintiff afforded sufficient evidence of a promise by him to pay interest in that manner.

67. The principle as regards the applicability of the rates, seems, therefore, to rest on the acquiescence of the debtor in the matter of calculation of interest at the contracted rate and the debtor needs, therefore, be estopped from denying its applicability. Since the matter of discretion of the Court in awarding interest on the principal sum is evidently within the discretion of the Court there is no necessity, however, to refer to any decision in this respect. Still, however the learned Counsel for the respondent Bank referred to the following decisions in support of the need for exercising discretion by the Court in favour of allowing interest at the agreed rate. Dr. Hossain referred to the following cases decided by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, namely, Panna Lal V. Nihai Chand, AIR 1922 PC 47, and Lala Hakim Rai V. Lala Ganga Ram, : AIR 1942 PC 61.

68. The respondent Bank claimed interest at the rate of 14% per annum on the principal sum for the entire period beginning from the date of filing the suit till realisation and it appears that the Court did not grant interest pendente lite at this rate but at the rate contracted in the agreement. The amount decreed by the Court is Tk. 6,31,10,307.13 includes the principle sum plus interest at the contracted rate. Dr. Hossain. Counsel for the respondent Bank submitted that though the Bank cannot as of right claim interest at the contracted rate for the period pending the suit. Courts have invariably awarded interest at such rate. In support of this proposition he referred to the following decisions reported in 1959 SCMR 690, 7 IA 196, : AIR 1933 Pat 207, : AIR 1934 Bom 86. Dr. Hossain pointed out that for the period beginning from the date of decree till realisation the Court did not grant interest at the rate claimed by the plaintiff but at 12% per annum which is a lower rate. According to him, the minimum rate of interest prevailing at the date of decree is seen to be provided on agricultural loans which was 10%, this being the concessional rate but the rate for ordinary advances is 15.5%, Vide, Bangladesh Bank Annual Report, 1980-81, at p. 36. Dr. Hossain asserted that if the Bank advanced such loan to other persons it could have earned interest at 15.5% per annum. Alternatively, if the appellant company had to borrow this amount from any other financial institution it would have to pay interest at a rate higher than 12% per annum which was awarded by the trial court. This is the minimum rate according to him and at this rate the trial court awarded interest to the Bank. Referring to the expressions "principal sum adjudged" which occur in Section 34 C.P.C. Dr. Hossain asserted that such expressions mean the principal sum together with interest accrued. In case of providing compound interest with quarterly rests, the principal sum is increased at the end of each quarter by the amount of the accrued interest upto date, and for the next quarter interest is calculated on this sum and this way it goes on until repayment in full is made.

69. In principle, what appears from Section 34 C.P.C. itself is that the Court is not bound by what is provided in the contract itself, the matter of awarding interest being completely within its discretion. So, in a case involving the award of interest on any dues outstanding against the debtor, the Court is free to award interest at such rate as it may think fit Ordinarily, that means if all that has happened to the loss of the appellant company were not there and the case would have been like any other loan transaction in normal circumstances, there would have been no objection to award interest on such principles. In the very extra-ordinary circumstances of the case without interfering with the principles enunciated by the aforesaid decisions as mentioned by the learned Counsel for the respondent Bank, we are reluctant to award any interest at all not only from the date of filing the suit till the date of the decree but for the entire period beginning from 13-12-71 to the date of the decree. The reason being the unmerited deprivation of the appellant company to enjoy not only his property and business rights but also utilization of the loan obtained from the Bank and the security offered against the loan by the Company. It is true that the Government has ultimately returned the appellant company to its former directors but even then excepting the amount of nearly Taka one crore which the administrator deposited in the Company's account in 1972, neither any sum by way of compensation not the equivalent amount of jute stocks were returned to the company. In this view of the matter we are reluctant to award any interest on the dues outstanding on 13-12-71 for the aforesaid period.

70. The controversy is as to what will be the rate of interest since the filing of the suit till the decree and then from the date of the decree till realisation. To determine this, it will be necessary to consider the provision Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is as follows:

34.-(1) Where and in so far as a decree is for the payment of money, the Court may, in the decree, Order interest at such rate as the Court deems reasonable to be paid on the principal sum adjudged, from the date of the suit to the date of the decree, in addition to any interest adjudged on such principal sum for any period prior to the institution of the suit, with further interest at such rate as the Court deems reasonable on the aggregate sum so adjudged, from the date of the decree to the date of payment, or to such earlier date as the Court thinks fit.

(2) Where such a decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest on such aggregate sum as aforesaid, from the date of the decree to the date of payment or other earlier date, the Court shall be deemed to have refused such interest, and a separate suit therefore shall not lie.

71. From the provisions of this Section it appears that the Court has been empowered to grant interest from date of the suit to the date of the decree and then of the full amount which includes the amount claimed on the date of the suit and the interest thereon granted by the Court for the aforesaid period. Further, the Section provides for award of interest on the aggregate sum till the date of realisation or an earlier date. It appears that the grant of interest from the date of the suit to the date of the decree and then from the date of the decree till realisation is a matter of discretion of the Court. This also find support from the opinions expressed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of bipradas Pal Chowdhury V. Kamini Kumar Lahiri, : AIR 1922 PC 48 and Lala Hakim Rai V. Lala Ganga Ram, : AIR 1942 PC 61.

72. On behalf of the appellant company Mr. M.M. Ispahani has admitted its liability regarding the loan upto 13-12-71. We have decided that the appellant company is liable to the Bank for the amount outstanding on that date and the respondent Bank can, therefore, validly ask for this amount from the company. This amount included both the principal sum and interest thereon calculated at the contracted rate. On 13-12-71 the actual amount outstanding is shown at Tk. 3,25,40,317.00 plus Tk. 33,00,000/- the total amount being Tk. 3,58,40,317.00. It has been seen that after taking over the appellant company the administrator deposited the amount of Tk. 99,00,000/- in the cash credit account of the appellant company. This amount should, therefore, be deducted from the amount outstanding on 13-12-71. On deduction 99 lacs therefrom the amount comes upto Tk. 2,59,40,317.00. This sum is adjudged as the principal sum outstanding on the date of filing the suit.

73. The next question come as to whether the Court will grant any interest on this amount for the period beginning from 13-12-71 to filing of the suit on 29-11-74. As the company came under total disability in the matter of operating its business as well as the Bank accounts for no fault of its own, it can legitimately ask for not granting any interest on the aforesaid outstanding dues for this period. It has been seen that the Bank also did not take any steps for clarifying its position regarding the repayment of the loan either from the company or from the Government during this period which it ought to have. We are, therefore, not in favour of awarding any interest for this period.

74. Even then the question remains whether the respondent Bank is entitled to award of interest on the outstanding dues during the pendency of the suit. Here, also, it is seen that the company did not get anything from the Government either by way of compensation or returning equivalent quantity of jute stocks which the company had in its stocks at the time of taking over. Though, of course, the company along with three subsidiaries companies had in the meantime been returned. It is true that Mr. M.M. Ispahani did not ask for any compensation from the Government instead of the jute stocks nor did he make the position clear regarding the repayment of loan from the respondent Bank. The fact remains that the Government has neither repaid the loan nor paid any compensation for taking over the jute stocks which the company claimed to have possessed on the date of taking over. This question has, in view, of the circumstances discussed above, lost its force, excepting its bearing in the matter of awarding interest its bearing in the matter of awarding interest for the period pendente lite. In all fairness, it must require to be said that there has not only been deprivation of property, but also destruction of the power and status of the appellant company to do jute business for which the loan was taken as well as of the security against which the same was taken. In these very special circumstances, the Court's discretion must be exercised in favour of the appellant company. We, therefore, disallow the interest on the aforesaid dues outstanding for the period during the pendency of the suit.

75. We however, award interest on the amount of Tk.k 2,59,40,317.00 as has been found to be due on 13-12-71 from the date of this judgment till realisation.

76. The appeal is allowed in p ART. The impugned decree is modified and the decretal amount is reduced to Tk. 2,59,40,317.00 (Taka Two crores fifty-nine lacs forty thousand and three hundred seventeen) only. In view of special circumstances of the case, the interest on this amount will be charged at the rate of 12% from to-day till realisation. There will be no Order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker, J.: This Rule was issued at the instance of the Plaintiff-Petitioner calling upon the Defendant-Opposite Party to show cause why the Judgment and order dated 12.9.80 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Sirajganj, in S.C.C. Suit No. 2 of 1978 dismissing the suit should not be set aside. 

2. The Plaintiff Petitioner instituted the aforesaid S.C.C. suit for evicting of the Defendant Opposite Party from the suit premises on the allegations, inter alia that the Plaintiffs arc the owners of the premises and the Defendant is a monthly tenant at a rental of Tk. 22. 50 on the basis of an agreement executed between the parties; that the Defendant is a habitual defaulter; that notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served upon the Defendant and that the premises is bonafide required by the Plaintiff. 

3. The Defendant-Opposite Party contested the suit by filing a Written Statement contending. Inter alia that the Plaintiffs were not owners of the property that he was not a tenant under the Plaintiffs nor he was a defaulter; that he is there in the premises on the basis of settlement from the Government and that the Government is a necessary party. 

4. An application under Order 1, Rule 10 C.P.C. was filed by the Government for being added as Defendant on the ground that the suit property situated within the periphery of Shajadpir, Pabna, and its ownership lies with the Government of Bangladesh. The Defendant-Opposite party supported the contention of the Government. The learned S.C.C. Judge in view of the contention raised by Government of Bangladesh claiming ownership of the property held that the Government was a necessary party to the suit and allowed it to be added as a Defendant. After addition of the Government as a Defendant the question arose as to the title and. possession of the suit property and the learned S.S.C. Judge found that there are complicated questions of title involved in the suit and as such the S.C.C. Court has no jurisdiction to try the suit. 

5. The learned S.C.C. Judge however held that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and, accordingly dismissed the suit as not maintainable. 

6. It is submitted by Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Petitioners that the learned S.C.C. Judge having arrived at the finding that complicated questions of title arc involved in the suit. it should have returned the Plaint for presentation to the proper Court and as such erred in law occasioning a failure of justice in dismissing the suit as not maintainable. 

7. Section 23 of the S.C.C. Act, 1887, provides that when the right of a Plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a Court of Small Causes depend upon the proof or disproof of title to immovable property, which such a Court cannot finally determine, the Court may, at any stage of the proceeding return the Plaint to be presented to a Court having jurisdiction to determine the title. Hence, the provision of Section 23 of the S.C.C. Act supports the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the Petitioners. The learned S.C.C. Judge after finding that the suit involved complicated questions of title should have returned the Plaint for representation to the proper Court. As such, the order of dismissal of the suit by the learned S.C.C. Judge is not sustainable in law. 

8. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The order of dismissal of the suit is set aside and the learned S.C.C. Judge is directed to return the Plaint to the Plaintiffs for presentation of the same to the proper Court. Since no body appeared on behalf of the Opposite Party, there will be no order as to cost.

9. Let the L.C. records be sent down to the Court below at once. 

End.

Raziur Rahman Chowdhury (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Badruzzaman J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why order dated 3-1-2013 passed by the respondent No. 3, in Arpito Sampatti Prottarpan Case No. 490 of 2012, adding respondent Nos. 5-8 as opposite party/defendants and order dated 18-2-2013 passed by the respondent No. 4 staying further proceeding of the aforesaid case till the disposal of CA No. 174 of 2011, pending before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh shall not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

2. Mr Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, learned Advocate, appearing in person submits that he is not willing to prosecute the 2nd part of the rule which is directed against the order dated 18-2-2013, staying further proceeding of the Case No. 490 of 2012 pending before the Tribunal. On the prayer of the petitioner the second part of the rule is discharged.

3. The first part of the rule is concerned about the legality of the order dated 3-1-2013 passed by respondent No. 3, adding respondent Nos. 5-8 as opposite parties in the case in question. Facts, in short, are that, the petitioner as plaintiff filed Arpito Sampatti Prottarpan Case No. 490 of 2012 before Arpito Sampatti Prottarpan Tribunal No. 2, Hobigonj against the government for release of the case property enlisted in serial No. 177 of Bangladesh Gazette published on 8-2-2012 as Arpito Sampatti (vested property). Government, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Hobigonj was contesting the case by filing written objection.

4. During pendency of the case respondent Nos. 5-8 as applicants filed an application on 3-1-2013 for being added as party in the case stating, inter alia, that the case property was leased out by the Government as yearly lease basis to one MA Motalib in VP Case No. 12 of 81-82 and while the said lessee was enjoying the case property died in the year 1994. After his death the petitioners, who are brother, daughter and other relatives of MA Motalib filed application on 9-2-2010 before the Deputy Commissioner, Hobigonj praying for granting lease in their favour and the matter was under consideration before the Deputy Commissioner. Therefore, they being necessary parties are required to be added as opposite parties.

5. The learned Judge of the Tribunal after hearing both the parties allowed the said application, impleading the respondent Nos. 5-8 as opposite party Nos. 2-5 in the case by the impugned order dated 3-1-2013.

6. Mr Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, in support of his case, submits that proposition presented by the phrases 'necessary party' or 'proper party' as contemplated in the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable in a case filed under Arpito Sampatti Prottarpan Ain, 2001 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Ain 2001') as section 4 of the Ain expressly restricts application of the Code in Arpito Sampatti cases and section 4 read with section 10(6)(As) of the Ain, 2001 clearly suggests that none but the Government, represented by the Deputy Commissioner is necessary party in such cases. There is, therefore, no scope for the respondents to be added as opposite parties in the Arpito Sampatti case in question. Apart from the above, Mr Rahman submits that even in ordinary cases the respondents are not entitled to be added as parties for the precise reason that they are admittedly not lessees in possession. He referred to the case of Babar Ali Pramanik vs Mosar Ali Pramanik, 45 DLR (AD) 120, in support of his point where it has been held that 'only lessees in possession are necessary parties in a suit against the lessor'.

7. Mr Md Shakhawat Hossain Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents No. 5-8 submits that the respondents are in possession of the case property since their predecessor, who was earlier lessee and after his death they filed an application before the concerned authority for granting fresh, lease of the property in their favour which is still pending for consideration, as such, the respondent Nos. 5-8 are proper and necessary parties in the case filed by the petitioner to release the property from the Gazette. Learned Advocate further submits that the learned Judge of the Tribunal committed no illegality in impleading the respondent Nos. 5-8 as opposite parties in the case and no interference is called for by this Court.

8. We have considered the submissions of the petitioner appearing in-person and learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents as well as perused the records of the case.

9. On scrutiny of the record, it appears that the case property was enlisted in the Gazette of Arpito Sampatti and the writ petitioner claiming ownership of the property filed the case for releasing the same. It is not denied that the Government granted lease of the property on a yearly basis to one MA Motalib in a VP Case and the possession of the property was handed over to him. It is also admitted that meanwhile the said lessee died. The claim of added respondent Nos. 5-8 is that after the death of the said lessee, they have been residing in the said property as successors and made application in the year 2010 for granting fresh lease in their favour, which is under consideration, as such, they have sufficient interest in the case property and are necessary parties in the case.

10. The question that pertinently arises now is that whether the Ain, 2001 excludes application of the Code of Civil Procedure and restricts all, except the Government from being added as opposite party in an Arpito Sampatti Case. We may aptly turn to sections 4 and 10(6) of the Ain, 2001. Section 4 and section 10(6) read as follows:

“৪। এই আইনের অধীন কোন কার্যধারায় দেওয়ানী কার্যৰিধির নিম্ন বর্ণিত বিধানাবলী ব্যতীত অন্য কোন বিধান প্রযোজ্য হইবে না, যথাঃ-

(ক) এই আইনে বা বিধিতে কোন বিষয়ে দেওয়ানী কার্যার্বিধির কোন বিধান যতটুকু প্রযোজ্য মর্মে বিধান করা হয় ততটুকু; এবং (খ) উক্ত কার্যবিধির ১১ ধারা ৷”

১০l …………….

(৬) এই ধারার অধীনে আবেদন প্রাপ্তির পর ট্রাইব্যুনাল-

(ক) অনধিক ৩০(ত্রিশ) দিনের মধ্যে উক্ত আবেদন এই আইন অনুযায়ী গ্রহনযোগ্য কিনা এবং আবেদনের সমর্থনে আপাতঃ দৃষ্টে পর্যাপ্ত কাগজপত্র দাখিল করা হইয়াছে কিনা তৎসষ্পর্কে সিদ্ধান্ত ও প্ৰয়োজনীয় নির্দেশ প্রদান করিবে,

(খ) আবেদনঢি গ্রহণযোগ্য হইলে সরকারের পক্ষে সংশ্লিষ্ট জেলার জেলা প্রশাসককে নোটিশ দিবে।

11. The above provisions of section 4 and section 10(6)05) of the Ain, 2001 suggests that except section 11, nothing of the Code of Civil Procedure will apply in Arpito Sampatti Cases unless such application is expressly provided in the Ain or Rules. It appears that the Ain, 2001 does not leave scope for any person other than the Government to be impleaded as party. Furthermore, section 10(6)(ক) of the Ain makes the intention of the law further clear, saying that, after acceptance of an application under the Ain, the Tribunal shall serve notice to the Deputy Commissioner to appear on behalf of the Government to contest the proceeding.

<u>12. The Ain, 2001 is a special law enacted for the special purpose empowering the Tribunal to ascertain as to the validity of inclusion of a property in the Gazette of Arpito Sampatti. The Ain specifically provides special procedure to be followed in the proceeding under the Ain overriding the applicability of the general provisions of the Code. Unless otherwise provided in the law there is no scope for the Court to add any person as party to the case. In view of the provision of section 4 read with section 10 of the Ain, we are of the opinion that the Tribunal has got no jurisdiction to entertain any application for addition of party, be that he is a lessee or lessee in possession. In a proceeding under Ain, 2001 the Government, represented by the concerned Deputy Commissioner is the only, necessary and proper party.</u>

13. The decision cited by the petitioner reported in 45 DLR (AD) 120 is all about a case where provisions of the Civil Procedure Code was applicable and thus clearly distinguishable from the case at hand.

14. For what we have stated above we are led to hold that the learned Judge of the Tribunal in passing the impugned order, has travelled beyond his jurisdiction and added the respondent Nos. 5-8 in the case in violation of law warranting interference by this court.

15. The first part of the rule, directed against order dated 3-1-2013, merits consideration which should be made absolute.

16. In the result the rule is made absolute in part. Impugned order dated 3-1-2013 is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

The order of stay granted earlier by this court is vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: By this Rule the opposite parties were called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 24-1-2006 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 209 of 2003 allowing the petition dated 10-10-2005 striking out the name of the defendant No.19 and also striking out the schedule No. 3 of the suit property from the plaint should not be set-aside.

2. The facts of the case as necessary for disposal of the Rule are that the opposite party No.1 as plaintiff filed a suit for partition and accounts in respect of the income of schedule-3 property in the Court of the then Sub-Judge, Dhaka on the averments that the plaintiff and her sisters and the defendants have been owing and possessing of the suit property in ejmali; that the properties have not been partitioned amongst the plaintiff and the defendants and for the various reasons it is very difficult to possess the suit property in ejmali; that since the properties have not been partitioned by Mets and bounds and it is very difficult for development of any part of the same the plaintiff has requested the defendant No. 1 for amicably settle the partition of the suit property but the defendant No. 1 deliberately on pretext refused to do the same and hence the suit.

3. The petitioner No. 1 as defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit and filled written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner inasmuch as all the parties are not added in the suit. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed an application under Order XI, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying to direct the defendant to supply the name of the necessary parties and thereupon, as per direction of the Court the defendant No. 1 supplied the name of one Haji Mohammad Sanaullah to be added as necessary party in the suit. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the materials on record by his order dated 15-3-1999 allowed the prayer of the plaintiff holding that the said Haji Mohammad Sanaullah is not a necessary party in the suit. Against which the defendant No.1 unsuccessfully moved a revisional application being Civil Revision No. 1473 of 1999 before this Court and then he went up to the Appellate Division and during tendency of the CPLA No. 698 of 2002 before the Appellate Division the plaintiff of the suit filed an application for imp leading the said Haji Mohammad Sanaullah as defendant in the suit and the learned trial Judge by order dated 24-10-2002 allowed the said application, in this way the said Haji Mohammad Sanaullah has been added as defendant No. 19 in the suit and consequently, the defendant-petitioner did not proceed with the CPLA No. 698 of 2002 before the Appellate Division.

4. In usual course the summon/s was served upon the added defendant No. 19, Haji Mohammad Sanaullah and thereafter, he appeared in the suit and on 10-10-2005 filed an application for striking out of his name from the suit and also striking out of the schedule property-3 from the suit property as described in the plaint.

5. The learned Joint District Judge by his order dated 10-10-2005 fixed the matter for hearing on 17-11-2005 with a direction to serve the copy of the application upon the parties. On 22-11-2006 the defendant No. 19 served a copy of the application dated 10-10-2003 to the learned Advocate of the plaintiff although the defendant No.19 did not serve any copy upon the contesting defendant No. 1 and thereupon, on 24-1-2006 the defendant No. 1 filed an application praying for a direction to the defendant No. 19 to serve a copy of the application dated 10-10-2005 to him and also for adjournment the hearing of the application dated 10-10-2005.

6. The learned Joint District Judge upon hearing the application of the defendant No. 1 (petitioner) was pleased to allow the said application as prayed for but subsequently, on the same day he took up the petition dated 10-10-2005 for hearing and upon hearing the learned Advocate for the added defendant No. 19 allowed the petition dated 10-10-2005 filed by the defendant No. 19 striking out of the name of the defendant No. 19 from the plaint and also striking out of the schedule property-3 of the suit property as described in the plaint.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 24-1-2006 the present defendant-petitioner has approached this Court in an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Golam Arshad, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that admittedly the plaintiff and defendant No. 1-4 transferred the schedule property-3 to the added defendant No.19 Haji Mohammad Sanaullah resulting he became a co-sharer to the suit property and in a suit for partition it is the mandatory provision of law that all the ejmali properties in between the co-sharers should be taken into hotchpots and since the schedule-3 of the plaint has not yet been partitioned by metes and bounds with the defendant No. 19 the learned Joint District Judge ought to have rejected the application for striking out the name of the added defendant No.19 Haji Mohammad Sanaullah from the suit and also for striking out of the schedule property-3 from the suit property

9. Mr Golam Arshad, the learned Advocate in the course of argument upon referring to the application dated 24-1-2006 along with impugned order dated 24-1-2006 submits that on 24-1-2006 the present petitioner as defendant No. 1 filed an application praying for a direction to supply the copy of the application filed by the defendant No. 19 and also for adjournment for submitting written objection and the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka upon hearing the application allowed the application as prayed for but the reasons best known to the learned trial Judge as to why on that date few minutes after he took up the application dated 10-10-2005 filed by the added defendant No. 19 for hearing in absence of the defendant No. 1 and mechanically allowed the same in a summary manner and as such, the impugned order is not only cryptic in nature also contrary to the first part of the impugned order which resulted in the failure of justice. The learned Advocate finally criticized the impugned order in submitting that in the facts and circumstances of the case the impugned order is perverse being contrary to law as well as the materials on record and, as such, the same is liable to be set-aside.

10. On the other hand, Mr MI, Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 by filing counter affidavit supports the impugned Order No. 104 dated 24-1-2006 which was according to him just, correct and proper. The learned Advocate in the course of argument upon placing the counter affidavit submits that the plaintiff as well as defendant Nos. 1-4 transferred their entire shares of schedule No. 3 of the suit property and in that view of the matter the defendant No. 19 is not a necessary party in the suit whatsoever. Mr Farooqui, the learned Advocate next submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case the impugned order is based on correct evaluation of facts and materials on record inasmuch as admittedly the plaintiff and defendant Nos.1-4 transferred their entire shares of the schedule property-3 to the added defendant No.19 Haji Mohammad Sanaullah. He further submits that the learned trial Judge after allowing the adjournment application of the defendant-petitioner took up the application dated 10-10-2005 for striking out the name of the defendant No. 19 from the plaint, which is a mere omission or irregularity, not an illegality and the law is well settled that mere omission or mere irregularity will not be a ground for interference when the order is otherwise supportable on merit.

11. Mr MI, Farooqui, finally submits that the order striking out the name of the defendant No.19 from the plaint has not occasioned any failure of justice inasmuch as in the facts and circumstances of the case the added defendant No. 19 is not a necessary party in the suit whatsoever and, as such, the question of interference by this Court sitting under revisional jurisdiction does not arise at all.

12. Perused the revisional application, counter affidavit along with Annexure as filed thereto and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties. It appears from the record that the defendant No.19 Haji Mohammad Sanaullah was made party as added defendant No. 19 pursuant to an application filed by the plaintiff on 24-10-2002 and thereafter, the said added defendant No. 19 appeared in the suit and filed an application for striking out of his name from the plaint and also for striking out the schedule-3 of the suit property as described in the plaint and the trial Judge on receipt of the application ordered to supply a copy of the same upon the parties and fixed the next date of the suit on 27-11-2005 and on that date the added defendant No. 19 filed hazira and the defendant No. 1 by filing application prayed for time which was allowed and thereafter, on 24-1-2006 the present defendant-petitioner filed an application for adjournment of the case on the ground for supplying a copy of the application dated 10-10-2005 to him and also for filing written objection and the trial Court below upon hearing the defendant No. 1 allowed the application of the defendant No. 1. Subsequently, on that date by the self-same order the trial Court below without hearing the contesting defendant No. 1 allowed the application dated 10-10-2005 filed by the added defendant No.19 for striking out the name of the added defendant No. 19 and also for striking out the schedule property-3 from the suit properties as described in the plaint.

13. Now, the only question for consideration is, whether the learned Joint District Judge has committed any illegality in passing the impugned order resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. To resolve this dispute we feel it necessary to quote hereunder the relevant portion of the application filed by the defendant Nos. 1 on 24-1-2006, which reads as follows:

১। অদ্য অত্র মোকদ্দমাটি দঃশুঃ জন্য দিন ধার্য্য আছে বটে।

২ ৷ ১নং বিবাদী অত্র মোকদ্দমা ১৯নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক দাখিলকৃত কপি প্রাপ্ত হয় নাই ৷ ১নং বিবাদীকে দরখাস্তের কপি দেওয়া হয় নাই৷ তদাবন্থায় ১নং বিবাদীর প্রতি দরখাস্তের কপি প্রদান করা আবশ্যক I কারন-১নং বিবাদী অত্র মোকদ্দমায় প্ৰতিদ্বন্দিকারী বিবাদী । ফলে ১নং বিবাদীকে কপি দাখিল সাপেক্ষে মোকদ্দমা দরখাস্ত শুনানী মুলতবী করিয়া আপত্তি দাখিলের জন্য সময় প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে৷ মঞ্জুর করা হউকI

14. The learned Joint District Judge upon hearing the application by its Order No.104 dated 24-1-2006 allowed the application stating as follows:

“১৯ নংবিবাদী পক্ষ হাজিরা দাখিল করিয়াছেন৷ বাদী পক্ষ হাজিরা দাখিল করিয়াছেন ৷ ১নং বিৰাদীপক্ষ এক দরখাস্ত দাখিল করতঃ দরখাস্ত বর্নিত কারনে সময় প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে। প্রার্থনা মঞ্জুর করা হইলl”

15. From the above, it is apparent that the prayer of the defendant No.1 was allowed but subsequently, the reasons best known to the learned Joint District Judge that as to why on the same date by the self-same order in absence of the present defendant-petitioner allowed the application dated 10-10-2005 filed by the added defendant No. 19 for striking out the name of the added defendant No. 19 from the plaint of the suit as well as striking out of his property namely, schedule property-3 as described in the plaint of the suit.

16. On the face of the impugned order, it appears that the first part of the order is totally inconsistent and contrary with the last part of the impugned order. Therefore, we are inclined to hold that the learned Joint District Judge seriously erred in law in passing the impugned order without properly applying his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject and the same has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.

<u>17. The Court cannot grant relief against the defendant or plaintiff either generally or otherwise which is inconsistent or contrary to its order. Granting of such relief against the defendant or plaintiff without affording opportunity to contest is not only violative of the principle of natural justice but also against judicial norms. Mr MI Farooqui, is not correct in submitting that the order striking out the name of the defendant No. 19 from the plaint as well as striking out the property namely schedule property-3 as described in the plaint of the suit has not occasioned any failure of justice.</u>

18. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order so far it relates to allowing the application dated 10-10-2005 filed by the added defendant No. 19 is set aside.

19. Since the matter has been dragging over a period of 10 (ten) years the trial Court is directed to expedite the trial of the suit in accordance with law.

Communicate the order at once.

End.
